CL002-077----:
On a narrow rock shelf covered by water-rolled stones and grass, extending E from the shore into Galway Bay NW of Ballyvaghan, known locally as ‘An Rinn’ (Robinson 1977). The site was reported to the National Monuments Service by Mr. Liam Moore of Ballyvaghan in 2007. It appears to be a small and largely buried wedge tomb. The visible elements comprise three capstones (L 0.75–1.1m; Wth 0.55–0.6m; T 0.15–0.25m) aligned ESE–WNW, starting at ground level and rising slightly to the WNW end (H c. 0.15m), and the tops of two orthostatic sidestones (L 0.5–0.6m; T 0.1–0.14m; H 0.22–0.26m) on the SSE side, under the two most WNW capstones. The top edges of the sidestones appear dressed like those at many other Burren wedge tombs. Two transverse stones (L c. 0.7m; T c. 0.15m) are partly visible beneath the WNW capstone. The site is locally known as ‘the Spanish Graves’ and believed to be the burial place of sailors from a wreck out in the harbour (Liam Moore pers. comm.).

CL003-037----:
Unobtrusively sited on a very gentle W-facing downslope c. 50m from the W shore of Aughinish island and obscured by a later E–W field wall which now forms part of its S side. Listed as an unlocated ‘Megalithic structure (possible)’ in the SMR (1992) but not listed in the RMP (1996). A small cist-like wedge tomb, open to the W and with an off-kilter rectangular capstone (L 1.85m E–W; Wth 1.5m; T 0.3m) supported by two smaller flagstones to the E (L 1m; H 0.8m; Wth 0.35m) and N (L 1.3m; H 0.7m; Wth 0.8m) and by a later wall along the S. Several small packing-stones are visible at the base of the N sidestone. The top of the E backstone and N sidestone appear dressed in the manner typical of many other Burren wedge tombs. The interior is partially filled with small stones cleared from the surrounding field.

CL004-016042-:
In the centre of an enclosure (CL004-016041-) within a slightly sunken linear depression orientated NNE-SSW.
A poorly preserved, probable wedge tomb comprising two upright slabs and three recumbent slabs and reported by Michael Lynch. The N stone (L 3.5m; H c. 0.75m) is located c. 2.2m from the S stone (L 1.3m; H c. 0.75m) and they appear to form the sidestones of a chamber orientated E-W. The largest of the recumbent slabs (L 1.7m; Wth 0.5m) rests on the N sidestone. A hut site (CL004-016043-) is located c. 10m to the NE.

CL004-066001-:
In a depression on a level karstic plateau, within a large multiperiod field system (CL004-027001-), with higher ground to the E and views of the ocean from SSW to NW. It is one of four wedge tombs (CL004-066001- and CL004-066002-, CL004-071---- and CL004-073----) known as the Ballynahown group in the Megalithic Survey (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 41). Westropp (1907, 462) recorded a ‘giant's grave…in a walled hollow’ with ‘rows of large stones, and entrance’. This may refer to this tomb which is located in a slight depression or it may refer to another wedge tomb (CL004-073----) c. 500m to the NE which is located in an oval hollow and is surrounded by a later stone wall.
A poorly preserved wedge tomb with a SSW-aligned chamber (est. min. L 3.6m; est. Wth c. 1.75m) which increases in height toward the front. It is on a low mound (est. diam. c. 7.5m) crossed by a NNE-SSW-oriented field wall c. 2.5m to the E of the chamber. The tomb was recorded in the Megalithic Survey as CL. 46 (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 40) (although the orientations cited in the written description are incorrect). The W side of the chamber comprises a single slab (L 3.6m; H 1.55m at SSW; H 1.45m at NNE; T 0.15m) with traces of dressing on its upper edge. A small, set slab (L 0.45m; H 0.25m; T 0.1m) located 1.75m to the E may be the broken base of an E sidestone. To the rear of the chamber are two parallel lines of slabs. The inner line comprises two E-W aligned slabs set end to end (W stone: L 1.2m; H 0.4m; T 0.15m; E stone: L 1m; H 0.3m; T 0.15m) 0.3m N of the W sidestone and the outer line, c. 1m to the N, comprises a single set slab (L 1.85m; H 0.2m; T 0.1m); both are likely remnants of outer wall lines. To the front of the chamber there are two small stones with similar dimensions (L 0.4m; H 0.1m; T 0.05m), set perpendicular and 1-1.5m beyond the W sidestone; these either mark the front of the chamber or an outer wall line. Two stones to the W of the W sidestone may also represent outer-walling (N stone: L 1.1m; H 0.2m; T 0.15m; S stone: L 0.8m; H 0.35m; T 0.1m). Further to the W of these stones is a small irregular upright (L 0.25m; H 0.45m; T 0.1m).
Field inspection in 1998 noted that the E sidestone, small front stones and low mound were no longer visible because of vegetation. Another wedge tomb (CL004-066002-) is located c. 91m to the N.

CL004-066002-:
On flat rocky ground with higher ground to the E and commanding views of the ocean from SW to NW over the Clare Coast and Galway Bay and within a large field system (CL004-027001-). It is one of four wedge tombs (CL004-066002-, CL004-066001-, CL004-071---- and CL004-073----) known as the Ballynahown group in the Megalithic Survey (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 41).
A poorly preserved wedge tomb with a SSW-aligned chamber (est. L c. 3m) which rises toward the front and is surrounded by a low mound (est. diam. c. 9.5m; H 0.6-0.75m). It was recorded in the Megalithic Survey as CL. 45 (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 40) (although the orientations cited in the written description are incorrect). The E side stone remains in situ (L 3.5m; H 1.3m at SSW; H 1.15m at NNE; T 0.1m); it is cracked towards the centre and the top edge is broken but traces of dressing are visible. A slab (L 3m; Wth c. 1.9m; T 0.1m), most likely the roofstone, leans against its W face.
Field inspection in 1998 noted that the interior is filled with large, flat stones. Long flat slabs incorporated into the nearby field wall c. 30m to the E may originally have formed part of the tomb. Another wedge tomb (CL004-066001-) is located c. 91m to the S.

CL004-071----:
On a broad rocky terrace in upland pasture within a large multi-period field system (CL004-027001-), with views over Galway Bay and the Aran islands to the W and sheltered by higher ground to the N. It is one of four wedge tombs (CL004-071----, CL004-073----, CL004-066002- and CL004-066001-) known as the Ballynahown group in the Megalithic Survey (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 41).
A well-preserved wedge tomb comprising a SSW-aligned chamber (L c. 2.5m; at SSW: Wth 1.3m; H 1.25m; at NNE: Wth 1.1m; H 1.15m) which increases in height and width toward the front and traces of a mound to the S. It was recorded in the Megalithic Survey as CL. 47 (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 41) (although the orientations cited in the written description are incorrect). The W and E sides of the chamber comprise single slabs (W slab: L 3.1m; H 1.3m at S; H 1.2m at N; T 0.1m; E slab: L 3.45m; H 1.15m at S; H 1.05m at N; T 0.1m), both of which are fitted into natural fissures in the bedrock, have dressed upper edges and tilt to the W. The backstone (L 0.95m; H 1.1m; T 0.12m) is dressed, especially on its the E corner. A stone (L 0.4m; H 0.2m; T 0.1m) c. 1m E of the chamber may be outer-walling. The roof-slab (L 2m; Wth 1.85m at N; Wth 1.80 at S; T 0.1-0.15m) is broken at its E and S extents and while it still sits on top of the tomb it does not appear to be in its original position. Within the chamber, natural bedrock is exposed and field inspection in 1998 noted that stones have been built up inside the chamber and extend to the N of it (L 2.5m). No trace of the mound was visible. An upright stone aligned E-W was recorded at the ESE extent of the wedge tomb and a low upright stone against the outer N face of the backstone was recorded. Modern drystone walling partially closes the S end of the chamber.
The other wedge tombs in the group lie c. 330m to the NW (CL004-066001-/CL004-066002-) and c. 490m to the NE (CL004-073----).

CL004-073----:
In an oval hollow on a high and level karstic plateau with restricted views but visibility of the Cliffs of Moher and the Aran Islands and within a large multiperiod field system (CL004-027001-). It is one of four wedge tombs (CL004-073----, CL004-071----, CL004-066002- and CL004-066001-) known as the Ballynahown group in the Megalithic Survey (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 41).
A poorly preserved wedge tomb with a SSW-aligned chamber (L c. 3.4m) which rises in height toward the front. There are traces of a cairn to its E and probably outer walling to the W of the chamber. It was recorded in the Megalithic Survey as CL. 44 (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 39-40) (although some of the orientations cited in the written description are incorrect). The W side of the chamber comprises a single slab (L 3.45m at base; H 1.25m at S; H 1.1m at N; T 0.15m) with a dressed and straight upper edge. A displaced slab (L 2.4m; T 0.1-0.15m) at the E end of the chamber overlies broken slabs which may have formed the S side of the chamber. A second displaced slab to the W of it (L 2.25m; T 0.1-0.15m) has similar dimensions and both slabs may have formed part of the roof. Two transverse stones with a gap between them (L 0.4m) cross the back end of the chamber. The outer stone (L 2.3m; T 0.1m; H 1.05m) leans to the E and has a broken top edge and the other stone is partially concealed (est. L 1.25m). A stone (0.45m; H 0.12m; T 0.1m) behind the outer N endstone at the rear of the chamber may be a buttress and another stone (L 0.75m; H 0.3m; T 0.1m) at the NW end of the chamber may not be original. Remains of outer-walling are visible along the W extent of the chamber. The longest stone (L 1.45m; H 0.12; T 0.05m) is parallel with the W sidestone and this line is continued to the N by a second stone (L 0.3m; H 0.1m; T 0.05m). Smaller stones beside this outer-walling may be further remains of outer-walling to the W of the chamber or may be cairn stones. A low stone wall (H 0.4m) surrounds the tomb SE to N; a gap in this wall at NW is lined by two set slabs which may have been reused from the wedge tomb.
The other wedge tombs in the group lie c. 480m to the SW (CL004-066001-/CL004-066002-) and c. 470m to the SSW (CL004-071----).

CL004-085----:
In a hollow in undulating landscape with cliffs (H c. 10m) overlooking the site c. 0.3-0.5m to the NE. The road is c. 30m to the W and a limestone erratic named ‘Cloch Bharr an Choinín’ on Robinson’s map (1977) is located c. 55m to the NNW.
A poorly preserved, rectangular cist with an E-W aligned chamber (int. dims. 3.85m E-W; 1.8m N-S) surrounded by a low cairn visible through the sod extending 2.8m to the N of the cist and 2.2m to the S. A gap (Wth 0.76m; L 0.45-0.55m) framed by two E-W aligned stones at W may be an entrance. The S side comprises three large stones (L 0.8-1.7m; H 0.6m), two of which lean inwards, with a fourth stone (L 0.65m) aligned NW-SE angled towards the potential entrance at W. The N side of the chamber comprises four stones of various lengths (0.12-1m) with two large gaps (L 0.7-1.2m) towards the W where stones may have been removed. The interior is slightly lower than the exterior and all the stones (int. H 0.1-0.3m) are generally flush with the ground outside or rise slightly over it. An area has been dug out at SE revealing an internal height of 0.6m for the most easterly stone on the S side. There are two stones (L 0.7m and 0.5m), aligned E-W towards the centre of the interior. A fulacht fia (CL004-085002-) is located c. 60m to the ESE.

CL005-003----: Situated inconspicuously on karst, in dense hazel scrub, on a valley floor E of Slieve Elva. A 3.2m high bench of rock rises 6m to the W and higher ground also rises to the N and E. A very overgrown wedge tomb. On inspection in 1997, it was not possible to photograph. It was overgrown but more easily recorded when surveyed by the Megalithic Survey (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 2) and the following details are from that report. The wedge tomb consists of an erect N sidestone (L 4.6m; H at W 1.4m; H at E 1.3m; T 0.25-0.45m), a recumbent and partially covered S sidestone (L 4.4m; W 1.7m; T 0.25m), a collapsed, cracked, partially covered roofstone (L 4.5m; W 1.75m; T 0.3m) and a standing but outwardly leaning backstone (L 1.15m, H 0.75m, T 0.15m) with an irregular upper edge. There are two similarly sized upright stones (L 1.30; H 0.7m) set in a line within the chamber, an apparently displaced but upright stone (L 0.9m; H 0.6m) leaning against the S endstone and several other moss-covered stones strewn about. It is not clear whether the upright stones within the chamber are original. The chamber appears to have been c. 3.75m long and orientated SW; its width at front or back cannot be determined. CL005-011----:
Within a large multiperiod field system (CL005-014001-), in rough grazing on a level terrace on the W side of a ridge which extends N from Gleninagh Mountain on the E side of the Caher Valley. There are extensive views over the valley and of Slieve Elva to the W.
A well-preserved wedge tomb consisting of a chamber (L 3.45m; Wth at rear 1.3m; Wth at front 1.7m; H at rear 1m; H at front 1.4m) and a parallel  outer wall to the S (L 8m; H at rear 0.6m; H at front 2m) built from large limestone slabs (De Valera & Ó Nualláin 1961, 1-2). Several low set stones and a sharp bank are the vestiges of an outer wall to the N.
The chamber’s sides are formed by very large stones overlapped by smaller parallel slabs set against the outer face of their W ends. There is evidence for dressing on the top of both of the larger sidestones. A broken capstone covers the W end of the chamber but the E end is now uncovered. The E end is closed by tightly fitted backstone and the W end of the chamber is partially closed by a broken stone set perpendicular to the chamber at the N corner, and a low sillstone traverses the gap between this and the S sidestone.
The S outer wall is set 0.5m from the S sidestone. It is parallel to and follows the pitch of the chamber. At its E end, a perpendicular stone partially closes the line between the rear of the S outer wall and the line of where the N outer wall ran, creating a wedge-shaped space to the rear of the chamber. This area is largely filled with small stones, and it is unclear whether or not it represents a rear chamber.
A modern wall, 12m to the E, creates shelter for animals and two turf thuiles are perched on the leading edge of a slightly higher ridge c. 90m SSE.

CL005-013001-:
Situated in rough grazing at the base of a N-facing slope, on the N-S ridge E of the Caher valley. A second wedge tomb (CL005-013002-) is located c. 35m ENE.
A collapsed wedge tomb that was not located on inspection in 1998. It was recorded by the Megalithic Survey (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 3) as ‘completely collapsed’ and as consisting of two sidestones with straight top edges, a capstone and three further recumbent slabs of unknown function. The capstone was described as an irregularly shaped slab (L 3.85m; T 0.1) that overlay the N sidestone (L2.9m; Wth at W 1.2m; Wth at E 1.25m; T 0.15-0.2m). The S sidestone (L 4.2m; Wth at W 1.3m; Wth at E 1.1m; T 0.15-0.2m) lay on one of the recumbent slabs (L 1.1m) and the remaining two recumbent slabs (L 1.85m & 2.4m) lay partially concealed in the ground W of the chamber.
Robinson (1977) marks the ‘hoofmarks of the Glas Ghaibhneach cow’, of the legendary smith Lon Mac Liofa, just SE of here.

CL005-013002-:
Situated in rough grazing at the base of a N-facing slope, on the N-S ridge E of the Caher valley. It was recorded by the Megalithic Survey  as CL.4 (de Valera & Ó Nualláin 1961, 3-4). Inspection in 1998 revealed it to be unchanged since the Megalithic Survey’s account. A second wedge tomb (CL005-013001-) is located c. 35m WSW.
Orientated towards the SSW, the wedge tomb (est. min. L 3.5m; Wth at W 2.1m) comprises a double-walled chamber surrounded by a mound (8m E-W; 6.5m N-S). The chamber is largely concealed by collapsed slabs that are likely displaced capstones. The N side of the chamber is defined by four stones (L 0.2-1.45m; H 0.2-0.65m) set in a line (L 3.2m) c. 0.5m inside the N outer walling; the longest and highest of those slabs is on the western end. The S side of the chamber is defined by three slabs (L 0.5-1.1m; H 0.2-0.25m) in a line (L 2.6m). Two slabs (L 1m & 0.4m; H 0.85m & 0.4m) are set in a line across the W end of the chamber. Immediately inside, or E of these are two slabs sat on edge but not set. Five displaced slabs (L 1-2.4m; Wth 0.7-1.6m) in the interior are likely parts of one or more capstones. The N outer wall is defined by a line (L 4.1m) of seven stones (L 0.3-0.9m; H 0.1-0.3m). Only two stones (L 0.2 & 0.7m; H 0.4 & 0.6m) survive along the line of the S outer wall. The W outer wall comprises three stones (L 0.9-1.35m; H 0.2-0.9m) set in a line c. 1.5m from the W end of the chamber. The top edge of the shortest is obviously broken and two slabs (L 1.75m & 2m, Wth 0.65m & 1m) lie on top of it. Two loose slabs (L c. 1.25m) lie in the area between the W end of the chamber and the W outer wall.
Robinson (1977) marks the ‘hoofmarks of the Glas Ghaibhneach cow’, of the legendary smith Lon Mac Liofa, just SE of here.

CL005-053002-:
On a NW-facing slope, under scrub and on the E side of Ballyvaughan valley. Indicated and named ‘Cromlech’ on the 1842 ed. of the OS 6-inch map and named ‘Cromlech (site of)’ on the 1916 ed. It was destroyed before Westropp’s time  (1901, 282) but was recorded in the O.S. Memoranda (1840) as ‘composed of large flags placed on four pedestals resembling a table of stone. The top 3 feet over the ground’ (DeValera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 92).
Inspection in 1998 failed to locate any surface trace of the monument. While the OS (1840) description is not sufficient to differentiate the class of this monument, it was almost certainly a megalith and probably either a portal or wedge tomb. The site of an enclosure (CL005-053001-) is located c. 10m to the SW.

CL005-091----:
At the head of a narrow valley in partially reclaimed pasture but with some scrub cover. Comprehensively recorded by the Megalithic Survey (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 5-6) but unlocated when inspected in 1999.
Described by the Megalithic Survey, as a moderately well-preserved, wedge-shaped tomb – in dense overgrowth - comprising a SW-orientated chamber (L 2.25m NE-SW; Wth at rear (NE) 1.25m; Wth at front (SW) c. 1.65m) surrounded by remnants of an outer wall (L c. 5m; Wth at front c. 4m) and a cairn (diam. c. 8m; max. H 0.5m).
The chamber consisted of northern and southern sidestones and a backstone. The S-sidestone (L 2.6m; T 0.1-0.3m) stood erect and had a flat top that rose steeply toward its front (H at rear 0.8m; H at front 1.25m). A small packing stone was set in the chamber near its rear end. The N-sidestone (L 2.35m) leaned out at a c. 45-degree angle and was consequently not as high (H at rear 0.75m; H at front 1m). The backstone (L 1.25m; H 0.8m) had both of its top corners removed and sat flush with the N-sidestone but there was a gap (Wth 0.1-0.2m) between it and the S-sidestone. There were two displaced stones, one S of the S-sidestone (L 0.8m) and another (L 1.25m) leaning on the backstone. Three slabs in the chamber (max. L 0.75m) may have been remnants of the capstone.
The tomb chamber appears to have been enclosed by a slightly larger, wedge-shaped outer wall (L c. 5m; Wth at front c. 4m). Seven slabs of the outer wall were recorded: a single slab (L 0.9m; H 0.35m) was set c. 1.1m behind the chamber’s backstone. Two slabs (L 0.95m; H 0.5m and L 0.55m; H 0.8m) survived to the N of the chamber’s N-sidestone, two more slabs to the S of the chamber’s S-sidestone (L 1m; H 0.4m and 1.15m; H 0.25m) and two slabs (L 1m; H 0.8m and L 0.8m; H 0.55m), set 0.35m apart, formed part of a flat façade to the front of the tomb.
The low, surrounding cairn was roughly circular (diam. c. 8m; max. H 0.5m) and there were some loose slabs (max. L 1m) lying to its W.

CL005-109----:
On level rough outcropping limestone karst and hazel-covered ground. The area to the E is extensively cleared.
A poorly surviving wedge tomb, heavily overgrown and difficult to distinguish at the time of inspection in 1997. The following is a summary of de Valera and Ó Nualláin’s (1961, 6-7) description. It is surrounded by a low mound (diam. 8m), crossed by an E-W field wall. Incorporated in this wall is the N sidestone (L 2.45m; if erect H 1.6m; T 0.2-0.25m) which leans S at an angle of c. 45֯. The N sidestone overlies two broken slabs. The W stone (L 1.7m; Wth 1.4m) has a dressed edge and is likely the W end of the S sidestone. The other (L 2.1m) overlies the W one and is likely the other part of the S sidestone. The broken base of the S sidestone (L 1.15m) is set beneath this. Three displaced slabs lie W of the chamber. The S of these (L 3.4m; Wth at W 2.6m; Wth at E 1.7m) is likely the roofstone. To the N of this is a slab (L 2.55m) of uncertain function. The third stone (exposed N edge L 1.3m) is incorporated in the fieldwall.
While de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) noted that the original dimensions of the chamber could not be ascertained, their plan indicates that it was orientated to the SSW and was likely c. 2.5m in length and c. 2.3m wide internally at the open W end, narrowing to c. 1.3m wide towards the rear. The surrounding mound may conceal the remains of a cairn, as exposed in the excavations of two of three wedge tomb (CL017-180002-) in Parknabinnia townland (Ó Maoldúin 2015). Another wedge tomb (CL005-110----) is visible in the neighbouring townland of Colleamore, c. 940m to the ESE.

CL005-110----:
At the S end of a short, low but moderately steep-sided ridge of pasture, with a good deal of rush cover and views to the S. Indicated and named ‘Dermot and Grania’s Bed’ on the 1842 and 1916 OS 6-inch maps.
The following details are from de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 10-11, attached). A moderately well-preserved wedge tomb, with a SW orientated chamber (L 3.1m; Wth at front 2.1m; Wth at rear 1.9m). The N sidestone (L 3.15m; H at front 1.95m; H at rear 1.45m; T 0.25m) is dressed along its upper edge and in situ, but leans S. The S sidestone survives as four set fragments (combined L 3.7m; H 0.1-0.3m; T 0.1-0.2m), S of which lie five slabs which suggest it was of similar dimension to the N sidestone. The backstone (L 1.6m; H 1.5m) is dressed along its upper edge and its upper S corner broken (D 0.3m); an irregularly shaped slab (H 1.55m) leans against its outer edge. A pillar-like stone (L 0.3m; T 0.2m; H 1.4m) stands against the E end of the N sidestone, three further stones (L 0.55-1.15m) lie in a line at the E end of the chamber and a block (L 1m; T 0.3m; H 0.2m) lies 0.7m to the W. Westropp (1907, 459) believed the block to the W of the chamber might indicate a longer chamber, but this is, as de Valera and Ó Nualláin’s (1961, 10-11) have pointed out, this is unclear. The site is abutted by E-W orientated post-medieval lazy beds on all sides. Another wedge tomb (CL005-109----) is visible in the neighbouring townland of Cooleabeg, 940m to the WNW.

On a level stretch of good grazing in an area with outcropping karst, within a multiperiod field system (CL005-227004-). The immediate views are restricted from N to S by a natural scarp c. 60m to the E. Indicated and named ‘Cromlech’ on the 1916 ed. of the OS 6-inch map and described as a ‘wedge-shaped gallery grave’ by Westropp (1907, 459).
The following details are from de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 8, attached). A poorly preserved wedge tomb with a just S of W aligned chamber (L 3.25m; Wth at rear 1.25m) set in an oval mound (9m E-W; 7m N-S). The only element of the chamber that remain in situ are the N sidestone (L 3.9m; H at front 1.15m; H at rear 0.7m; T 0.1-0.2m), the E end of the S sidestone’s base (L 0.8m; H 0.2m) and a damaged backstone (L 1.25m; H 0.5m). Well-set stones, c. 0.35m to the N (L 0.75; H 0.12m) and S (L 0.5m; H 0.15m) of the E end of the chamber and to its SW (L 0.35m; H 0.13m) may be remnants of an outer wall.

CL005-129----:
On generally level mixed rough pasture and exposed limestone pavement, with land rising slightly to the N but wide views elsewhere, and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL005-227004-). Listed as a wedge tomb by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1989, 134). This mostly collapsed tomb is orientated E-W, and is embedded in the centre of a subcircular mound (5.5m N-S; 5.5m E-W; H 0.65-0.8m). Some loose stones along the mound’s N side may be part of a later field wall which runs ENE-WSW across the monument. The tomb survives as an E-W line of three collapsed capstone slabs. The E slab (L c. 1.8m; Wth 1.4m; T 0.1-0.14m) has an E-W crack through it. The middle capstone (L 1.7m; Wth 1.7m; T 0.1-0.2m) is cracked into three pieces at its E end, suggesting that perhaps this capstone and that to the E are two broken parts of a single fragmented slab. A third capstone slab (L 2m; Wth 1.35m; T 0.2m) lies partly beneath the SW end of the middle slab. Just S of the middle capstone piece is a tilted but earthfast upright slab (L 1.45m; min. H 1.1m; T 0.07-0.12m), orientated E-W, which may be part of the tomb’s S side. Another upright stone may be part of the tomb’s N side; however, it is mostly covered by the N edge of the E fallen capstone slab. Some 3m W of the W capstone piece—i.e., beyond the mound—is a small, upright stone (L 1.5m; min. H 0.7m; T 0.2m) orientated-S which tilts to the W. There is a cist (CL005-217----) 6m to the NNE, and another cist (CL005-218----) 86m to the ENE.

CL005-133----:
On a very slight rise in mixed rough pasture and exposed limestone pavement, overlooked by higher land to the S and W and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL005-227004-). Marked as ‘Cromlech’ on the OS 25-inch plan (1897) and Cassini edition (1920) of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 12) as a well-preserved wedge tomb (L 2.8m; Wth 0.95m at NE, 1.3m at SW; H 1.1m at NE, 1.3m at SW) orientated NE-SW and embedded in the centre of a kidney bean-shaped mound (8m NE-SW; 5m NW-SE; H 0.5m). During an inspection in 1998 the SW side of this mound was found exposed as a stony cairn. According to de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.), the NW and SE sides of the tomb each comprised a single limestone slab set on its long edge. The SE sidestone (L 3.4m; H 1.15m at NE, 1.35m at SW; av. T 0.25m) was intact but the NW sidestone (L 3.25m; H 1.1m at NE, 1.3m at SW; av. T 0.25m) had a rectangular piece (L 0.6m; H 0.45m) missing at its top NE corner. Both sidestones’ straight, fairly flat top edges bore signs of dressing and sloped evenly to the SE. A vertical abrasion mark on the inner face of the NW sidestone, 0.8m from its NE end, was thought to possibly indicate the former position of the chamber’s missing NE endstone. Outside the NE end of the NW sidestone was a stone on edge (L 0.5m; H 0.3m; T 0.1m) which may have been a packing stone. This was not located during the 1998 inspection. Extending the line of the SW sidestone to the NE was a low slab (H 0.25). The SW end of the chamber was blocked by two upright slabs, one (H 1.25m; Wth 0.6m; T 0.15m) to the S which was firmly set, and another (H 1.25m; Wth 0.6m; T 0.15m) set askew, tapered to a point and considered to be a possible doorstone. The irregular capstone (L 3.3m, Wth 1.9m at NE, 2.25m at SW; T 0.25m) rested on the sidestones and the S of the two blocking-stones at the SW end of the chamber. Within the chamber were three small packing-stones (H 0.05-0.1m) against the SE sidestone which were not located during the 1998 inspection. Rather, loose flat stones filled the floor of the tomb chamber. Michael Gibbons (2007) discovered rock art (CL005-133002-) on the inner face of the NW sidestone: 4-6 tool-pecked cupmarks (diam. 1-2.5cm; D 1-1.5cm) and another on the inner face of the SE sidestone. The cupmarks were studied by Dr Blaze O’Connor (UCD) who confirmed that they are anthropogenic (ibid.). She found no dating evidence but suggested that the largest cupmark with its slightly pointed base (probably made with a metal tool) is not typical of prehistoric examples, suggesting later activity.
This is the southernmost of three closely associated wedge tombs along with a second (CL005-135----) c. 165m to the NNE and a third (CL005-136001-) c. 100m beyond again. The famous Gleninsheen gorget and a bronze armlet (National Museum of Ireland register 1938:8587) were found c. 485m to the E.

CL005-135----:
On a very slight rise in mixed rough pasture and exposed limestone pavement, overlooked by slightly higher ground to the S and W. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 9) as a considerably broken and disturbed wedge tomb (est. L 3.3m; Wth 1.25m at E, 1.8m at W), orientated E-W and embedded in a barely traceable oval-shaped mound (c. 9.5m E-W; est. 6m N-S; max. H c. 1m). A later field wall extends E and W from the mound, on which de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) noted then recently damaged flat slabs. The upstanding S sidestone (L 4.25m; H 0.95m at E, 1.2m at W; T 0.2-0.3m) was dressed on its straight top edge, while its E and W side-edges were quite straight but undressed. There was a thin vertical crack near the centre of this slab. Only a small piece (L 0.9m; 0.2m; T 0.25m) of the N sidestone remained upstanding; a flat slab (L 2.15m) on the N part of the mound may be the rest of this sidestone. A small stone (L 0.85m; H 0.6m) orientated N-S between the upstanding sidestones was thought to possibly mark the W end of the chamber. De Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) considered two tall tapering stones (H 1.4-1.55m; L 0.7-0.9m) just W of this endstone to most likely be related to the later field wall at the mound. Among other prostrate slabs on the mound, some may be fallen endstones from the E end of the chamber; Westropp (1899, 381) found both ends still standing. A large irregular slab (L 2.2m) at the S side was suggested by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) as possibly part of the tomb’s capstone. Westropp (ibid.) noted that the monument was ‘perfect’ in 1862. Approximately 100m to the NNE is a wedge tomb (CL005-136001-), while c. 165m to the SSW is another (CL005-133----). The famous Gleninsheen gorget and a bronze armlet (NMI 1938:8587) were found c. 440m to the E.

CL005-136001-:
In partly hazel-covered rough pasture. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 8) as a notably small wedge tomb (L c. 2.5m; max. Wth c. 1m at W; H 0.65m), orientated NE-SW and embedded in a grass-covered oval mound (c. 10m E-W; 7.5m N-S; H 1.2m) of stones and reddish clay. Several possible kerbstones protruded from the mound. There was a recently made hole (D 0.5m) on the mound’s N side. The remains of the tomb chamber comprised two sidestones (NW sidestone L 2.8m; H 0.85m; T 0.1m; SE sidestone L 2.6m; H 0.85m; T 0.1-0.15m) set on edge but leaning in toward each other (top edges 0.35m apart at SW, 0.25m apart at NE). Both slabs have straight top edges which curve downward at their NE ends, while their SW ends are covered by a modern drystone wall which also blocks the SW end of the chamber. The uneven chamber floor slopes to the SW. During an inspection in 1998, the SW part of the hazel-covered chamber was found covered by two flat slabs (L 0.6-0.65m; Wth 0.45-0.6m; T 0.05m).   It was also possible to make out most of the outline of the retaining mound (max. H 1m), with two loose flags on its S side. Approximately 100m to the SSW is another wedge tomb (CL005-135----), and there is another (CL005-133----) c. 165m beyond this to the SSW.

CL005-143----:
In elevated pasture on the S-facing slope of Ballyallaban Hill with clear views from SE to SW. Within a multiperiod field system (CL005-104001-). Indicated and named ‘Cromlech’ on the 1839 and 1916 OS 6-inch maps. A well-preserved wedge tomb aligned E-W and centrally placed within a grassed-over cairn. The following details are derived from de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 7). The tomb comprises a N sidestone, the remains of a S sidestone, a W doorstone, and single large roofstone, defining a wedge-shaped chamber (L 4m; H 0.9-2m; Wth 0.9-1.3m) broadest and highest to the W, and narrowing and lowering to the E. The N sidestone (L 3.75m; H 1.95m; T 0.1-0.25m) leans slightly outwards and is vertically cracked c. 1.5m from its E end. Its upper edge is dressed and slopes sharply down to the E. Small packing stones are visible along the base of the stone. The S sidestone survives only as two ex-situ slab fragments propped along the S side of the tomb. Both fragments appear to derive from the broken sidestone, which Westropp noted had ‘collapsed since 1862’ (1899, 381). The W slab (L 1.4m; H 1.35m; T 0.25m) has a straight top edge, but its other edges appear broken. A second slab fragment to the E (L 1.65m; H 1.15m; T 0.15m) also appears to be derived from the broken sidestone. The S side of the tomb has been partially built up with drystone walling from a boundary flanking the S side of the monument. The W end of the chamber is closed by a cracked doorstone (L 2.1m; H 1.85m; T 0.1-0.2m), on which the roofstone now rests. The roofstone (L 4.25m; Wth 0.9-1.95m; T 0.2m) widens from E to W and is cracked c. 0.75m from its E end. A well-set slab (L 0.65m; H 0.6m; T 0.1-0.15m) runs partially across the E end of the chamber.
The tomb is set within a cairn (c. 8m N-S; c. 10m E-W; H 0.7m), which has been partially quarried to the S. Four upright slabs (L 0.4-1.2m; H 0.1-0.5m) are set within the cairn W of the doorstone. They may be the remnants of a stone kerb or be related to a later field wall which abuts the cairn.

CL005-160016-:
In elevated rocky pasture on a SW-facing slope with clear views to the W from Poulawack to Cappanawalla and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL005-160001-). Indicated and named ‘Cromlech’ on the 1840 and 1916 OS 6-inch maps. Described by Westropp (1899, 373) as a ‘fallen cromlech’ and classified by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1962, 13) as a ‘wedge-shaped gallery grave’. The details that follow are from de Valera and Ó Nualláin.
A collapsed wedge tomb orientated ESE-WNW set centrally within a low oval mound. The monument comprises a roughly trapezoidal capstone, widest at WNW and narrowing to ESE (L 3.45m; Wth 1.8-2.3m; T 0.15-0.2m), lying on top of the fallen sidestones. The sidestones are represented by four large broken slabs, three lie on the N side of the capstone, with one to the S. Only two of the N slabs are clearly visible (W stone Wth 1.8m; T 0.1-0.15m; E stone Wth 1.5m; T 0.1-0.15m), concealing a third fallen slab beneath. A single slab (L 1.55m; T 0.1-0.15m) is visible to the S. A low upright stone at the W end of the chamber (Wth 1.2m; H 0.3m) may be the base of a doorstone.
The mound (8.5m E-W; 6.6m N-S; H 0.75m) is grassed over with poorly defined edges. Five protruding upright stones suggest the presence of kerbing and/or internal walling in the mound. Two stones, one to the SW (Wth 0.8m; H 0.15m; T 0.1m) and one to the SE (Wth 0.35m; H 0.1m; T 0.07m), appear to represent an inner wall. Three stones to the NW, SW (Wth 0.6m; H 0.4m; T 0.15m) and SE (Wth 1.2m; H 0.45m; T 0.15m) appear to represent an outer wall or kerb.
A cross has been incised with a small hollow (L 0.15m; Wth 0.07m) on the centre of the capstone suggesting the reuse of the tomb as altar or mass-rock (CL005-310----). Westropp (1899, 373) and de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 13) noted the presence of a small stack of stones on the top of the capstone holding an upright slab shaped like a ‘round-headed cross’ or ‘a rude human figure’. On inspection in 1998 the stack of stones remained, but the upright slab was not present.
The N edge of the mound is overlain by the drystone wall of a subrectangular enclosure. The wedge tomb and mound were incorporated into a mound wall aligned ENE-WSW and coaxial with a rectangular cashel (CL005-160010-) located c. 70m to the SW.

CL005-160018-:
In elevated rocky pasture with extensive views to the W and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL005-160001-). Indicated and named ‘Cromlech’ on the 1840 and 1916 OS 6-inch maps. The former map indicates a mound surrounding the monument. Noted by Westropp (1899, 373) as a ‘cromlech’ ‘in the remains of a mound on a heathy moor … made of three very thin slabs’. Classified by de Valera and Ó Nualláin as a ‘wedge-shaped gallery grave’ (1962, 14) and the details that follow are taken from there.
A well-preserved wedge tomb orientated ENE-WSW and set within an oval grass-covered cairn (9m E-W; 7m N-S; H 1m). The tomb comprises a capstone (L 2.1m; Wth 1.9m; T 0.15m) supported by a N sidestone (L 2.35m; H 1.15m; T 0.15-25m) and a S sidestone (L 3m; H 0.95m; T 0.1m). The top edges of both sidestones slope down to the E and exhibit traces of dressing. The N sidestone leans slightly inwards, and part of the upper surface of the S sidestone appears to have broken off. According to Westropp (1911, 355) the capstone was pushed S between 1899 and 1911. It now rests with its S edge against the top of the S sidestone with its N edge protruding c. 0.35m beyond the N sidestone. The chamber is broadest and highest to the SW (Wth 1.2m) decreasing in height and width to the NE (Wth 1.15m). On inspection in 1998 the tomb was found to be unchanged since de Valera and Ó Nualláin’s visit. The wedge tomb and mound are incorporated into a sinuous mound wall aligned broadly E-W.

CL005-160027-:
In elevated rocky pasture, on an E-facing slope near the E edge of a large limestone plateau, with a sheer precipice c. 170m to the E, and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL005-160001-). Not shown on the 1839 or 1916 OS 6-inch maps. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 9-10) as a ‘wedge-shaped gallery grave’. The following details are from that survey.
A wedge tomb orientated N-S comprising the remains of two large side sidestones, a backstone and a broken doorstone defining a rectangular chamber (L c. 3.2m; Wth c. 1.6m) set within a low mound (c. 7.5m N-S; c. 5.5m E-W). The E sidestone consists of two large fragments of the same slab (L 4.3m). The S fragment is in-situ (L 2.12m; H 1.15-1.35m). Its top edge slopes down to the N and is dressed. The N fragment has collapsed. The W side of the chamber is composed of two fragments of stone, representing the remains of a single cracked slab, the N fragment (L 2.3m; H 1.1m; T 0.1m) being slightly larger than the S fragment (L 1.65m; H 0.3m; T 0.1m). The top edges of both stones are badly broken. The backstone (L 1.5m; H 1.2m; T 0.2m) is at the N end of the tomb. Its top and W edges are dressed. The S end of the chamber is defined by two low stones that taken together represent part of a broken doorstone (L 1.1m; H 0.12m; T 0.08m). The chamber is parallel sided, being higher at the S (H 1.35m) and lower towards the N (H 1.2m). Three low stones (H 0.05m) set beyond the S end of the E sidestone may be packing or the remains of outer walling. Several partly concealed slabs (max. dims. L 1m; Wth 0.75m) lie outside the chamber and may be remnants of the capstone.

CL005-161----:
In elevated improved pasture on a gentle W-facing slope, abutting the Cragballyconoal-Ballymihil townland boundary and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL005-160001-). Named ‘Cromlech’ on the 1839 and 1916 OS 6-inch maps, with a mound indicated by a dashed line on the former map. Called the ‘White Labba’ by Westropp (1906-7, 460), and described as ‘a cromlech in a green mound; the top has been removed since 1862 … the top edges have been hammer-dressed; they slope towards the east, and being coated with white lichen form a conspicuous object across the valley’ (1899, 372).
Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1962, 14-15) as orientated NE-SW and comprising a NW sidestone (L 4.2m; H 1.3-7m; T 0.25-0.3m), a SE sidestone (L 3.7m; H 1.3-7m; T 0.25-0.3m) and an NE backstone (Wth 1.8m; H 1.05m; T 0.2m) set within a ‘long distorted mound’ (19m E-W; 13m N-S; max. H 1.5m), augmented by dumped field rubble. The sidestones had straight dressed top edges which sloped down from SW to NE. The chamber (L c. 3m) was widest at the SW (Wth 1.75m), narrowing slightly to the NE. No trace of the monument was evident on inspection in 1998. A large limestone flag possibly representing the remains of the tomb is visible on OSi MapGenie orthophotography (2013-2018) and on Google Earth (25 April 2021) lying recumbent beside a drystone field wall c. 10m NE of the original site of the monument. A mound (CL005-182----) lies c. 130m to the SW.

CL006-035003-:
On rough grazing near the upper edge of a steep NE-facing slope with panoramic views over the valley beyond and Turlough Hill cairn (CL006-017002-) c. 6.5km NNE. A well-preserved single-chambered SSW-orientated wedge tomb (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 15–16), centrally placed in a roughly circular cairn (diam. c. 9m). The tomb chamber (L 2.4m) comprises 4 orthostats (2 sidestones, a backstone and a sillstone) and a capstone, and widens and rises toward the SSW end (Wth at NNE 1.2m; Wth at SSW 1.25m; H at NNE 1.05m; H at SSW 1.3m). The N sidestone (L 3m; max. exposed H 1.3m; T 0.15–0.25m) leans very slightly outward; its upper edge is stepped, squarish in section and appears undressed. The S sidestone (L 3.35m; max. exposed H 1.3m; T 0.15–0.25m) leans slightly inward; its upper edge is rounded and appears undressed. The backstone (L 1.2m; exposed H 1.3m; T 0.2m) is neatly fitted with its sides almost touching the sidestones and with the capstone resting on its upper edge. Its upper edge is dressed and a quarter circle ope (L 0.35; Wth 0.3m) has been worked into its top N corner. Its top S corner has also broken away (L 0.4m; Wth 0.35m) but with less evidence of human intention. The sillstone (L 0.8m; exposed H 0.45m; T 0.1m) is firmly set, slightly askew of the chamber, leans inward and its upper edge is worn smooth. There is a gap between it and the S sidestone (0.35m) and between its upper edge and roofstone (Wth 0.75m). The capstone (L 3.25m; T 0.2–0.3m) sits on both sidestones and the backstone. It is wider at its SSW end (Wth 1.8m) than its NNE end (Wth 1.45m), but the SE end does appear to have been cut away and an incised line along its S edge may be of recent origin. A line of stone slabs (L 0.2–0.8m; av. H 0.2m) within the cairn, forms an arc from WNW to ENE c. 2m N of the tomb. This may be part of the cairn structure or an internal kerb defining a phase of construction. A grassed-over mound wall runs WSW off the cairn. It, other mound walls and slab walls traversing the field form part of a multiperiod field system (CL005-160001-) that extends over the plateau to the W and into the neighbouring townlands of Cragballyconoal and Eanty More. Two grassed-over cairns (CL006-035001- and CL006-035002-) the first of which contains a cist (CL006-035004-), are located c. 20m NW and 70m NW respectively.

Towards the S leading edge of a terrace of rough patchy grazing and bare rock pavement, in a valley between Gortaclare and Doomore mountains. A small WSW orientated and poorly preserved wedge tomb (chamber L 1.8m; Wth indeterminable) set in a low roughly circular mound (diam. 7m). The S sidestone (L 2.05m; H 1.05; T 0.15m) survives in situ but leans outward. Its upper edge is dressed and when in its original position it would have risen toward the WSW. A smaller stone (L 0.9m; H 0.85m T 0.1–0.25m) at the W end of the N side may be a remnant of the N sidestone. The backstone (L 1.15m; H 0.8m; T 0.15m) also remains in situ at the E end of the chamber. There are two stones at the E end of the chamber; a blocking stone (L 1.05m; H 0.75m; T 0.15m) and a second smaller parallel stone (L 0.85; 0.35m; T 0.1m), set some 0.4m further W. The smaller stone is likely a displaced doorstone. The capstone (L 1.5m; Wth 1.4m; T 0.1m) sits on the E end of the chamber and rests on the S sidestone, the backstone and the stone at the W end of the N side. When Westropp (Comber 2004, 60) recorded it there were two capstones. He also recorded a ‘curious little stone, shaped like a rough cross’ within it, of which there is no sign today (ibid.).
The tomb is located at the centre of an extensive multiperiod field system (CL006-042001-) that encompasses three enclosures or ‘prehistoric farmsteads’ (CL006-098002-, CL006-144---- and CL006-146----) (Carey 2009). Comparisons with the dated enclosures or ‘farmsteads’ on Roughan Hill suggest that these and some of the mound walls of the field system (CL006-042001-) are likely contemporary with the wedge tomb (Jones et. al. 2011; Jones 2016). A complex of hut sites and small enclosures (CL006-042008-) are located c. 60m to the W.

CL006-052----:
On rough level karst and patchy grazing. The ground falls gently away to S and W and rises gently to E. A low ridge in next field to N limits the aspect. A poorly preserved wedge tomb on a low grass-covered cairn (ext. dims 6.1m NE–SW; 4.5m NW–SE; max. H 0.4m) which has been robbed out at NW. All that survives of the wedge tomb in situ is one large NE–SW orientated sidestone (L 2.8m; H at SW end 1.3m; H at NE end 0.4m; T 0.16m) supported by two small slabs (L 0.86; H 0.4m; T 0.07m and L 0.8m; H 0.1m; T 0.05m) set perpendicularly on its NW side. The lower NE end of the sidestone is broken and a fragment rests on one of the perpendicular supporting stones. Three slabs (combined length 3.36m) located c. 5m NW may be the remains of another sidestone.

CL006-056----:
In a small clearing surrounded by moderately dense hazel scrub in an area of rough outcropping rock. A tomb is indicated and named ‘Cromlech’ in this area on both the 1842 and 1915 eds. of the OS 6-inch maps. However, on the 1842 map it is located c. 100m to the S. Perhaps because of the mapping discrepancy and the dense hazel, on his initial visit to Rannagh East Westropp (Comber 1999, 60) did not manage to find this tomb and instead recorded a tomb (CL006-057----) in Termon as in this townland. However, he later corrected his mistake and did record this tomb (Comber 1999, 110–11). It is listed and described in the Megalithic Survey as CL.21 (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 16–17).
It is a poorly preserved wedge tomb set in a low mound (12.5m NE–SW; 11m NW-SE), of which only two broken sidestones and two possible chamber endstones survive. It is orientated SW and the sidestones diverge (chamber Wth at E end 1.9m; chamber Wth at W end 2.55m) and rise (see southern sidestone) in that direction. The southern sidestone (L 4.55m; T 0.2–0.4m; H at NE 1.3m; H at SW 1.4m) survives largely intact but its upper NE end is broken, it is cracked in three places and it leans outward. Its upper edge is dressed to a rounded shape and its SW upper edge juts forward in a ‘prow’. All that remains of the northern sidestone are three pieces, the largest and best preserved of which is its SW end (L 2.9m; H at W end 1.45m, H at E end 1.4m). This is not as definitively dressed as the southern sidestone, but some chips do appear to have been removed. Its upper edge is squarish, and its SW end projects in a ‘prow’, like the southern sidestone; the two other surviving pieces (L 0.7m and 0.4m) suggest it was once as long (c. 4.5m) as the southern sidestone. The possible endstones overlap one another in the west end of the tomb. The more northerly (L 1.3m; H 0.95m; T 0.15m) is set outside the more southerly (L 0.95m; 0.35m; T 0.35m). The smaller southerly stone may have acted as a sill and served to allow access to the tomb. Six small stones (H 0.1–0.2m) form a line (L c. 3m) running SW–NE along the NW side of the tomb. The most north-easterly stone is set perpendicular to the line potentially making a terminus. A later field wall extends SE from the SE side of the tomb.
Another wedge tomb (CL010-019----) is in Rannagh East c. 510m to the SSW and the wedge tomb (CL006-057----) in Termon townland is located c. 300m to the ESE.

CL006-057----:
On a low craggy W-facing slope on the E side of a N–S valley with views of wedge tomb CL006-056----c. 300m to WNW. Indicated on the 1842 and 1915 eds. of the OS 6-inch maps and named ‘Dermot & Grania’s Bed’ on the 1915 ed. Westropp (Comber 1999, 60) initially recorded it as in Rannagh East, but later corrected his mistake (Comber 1999 , 110-11). It is recorded in the Megalithic Survey as CL.22 (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 17–18).
A well-preserved wedge tomb set in a grass-covered mound (9m N–S; 7m E–W; H 1m). Stones protruding from the mound suggest it may be composed of small overlapping slabs, like those recorded elsewhere (Ó Maoldúin 2015). The tomb is orientated just W of S and both sidestones and capstone remain in situ. The chamber widens and rises toward the south (L 2.9m; Wth at N 0.8m; Wth at S 0.9m; H c. 1m). The sidestones are of similar dimension (L 2.9m; T 0.25m; H at S 0.95m) and their upper edges are dressed. The W sidestone has a narrow crack 0.6m from its S end. The E sidestone leans slightly inward and has a thin incised line along its inside, 0.13m from its top edge, that de Valera and Ó’Nualláin believed to be a modern attempt to remove a part of it (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 17). The capstone (L 2.45m; Wth at S 1.6m; Wth at N 1.3m) rests on the W sidestone at two points and on the E sidestone at only one. A stone (L 0.5m; H 0.15m; T 0.15) outside the S end of the E sidestone may have been a packer and a recumbent stone (0.7m x 0.7m; T 0.2m) at the south end may have blocked the end of the chamber.

CL006-060----:
On a narrow terrace set into a steep SE-facing slope of rough rock and patchy grazing. Recorded in the megalithic survey as CL. 23 (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 18).
A well-preserved wedge tomb set in a mound (7.5m E–W; 5.5m N-S) at which three walls of some antiquity converge. The chamber (L 3m) is orientated SW and rises and widens in that direction (Wth at NE 0.75m; Wth at SW 0.95m; H at NE 0.5m; H at SW 0.65m). It is partially filled and embedded within the mound, so the true height is probably considerably more. The NW sidestone (L 3.05m; H at NE 0.45m; H at SW 0.6m; T 0.15–0.25m) is cracked through 1.3m from its SW end. The SE side has two sidestones which may originally have been one. The larger (L 2.35m; H at NE 0.5m; H at SW 0.65m; T 0.1–0.15m) of the SE sidestones is at the SW end of the chamber and is also cracked through, 1.75m from its SW end. The smaller (L 0.6m; H 0.45m; T 0.1m) is at the NE end. There are two capstones, a large one (L 2.35m; Wth at W end 1.25m; Wth at E end 1m; T 0.25m) on the SW end and a smaller one (L 0.9m; Wth 0.45m; T 0.15m) on its NE end. There are some loose slabs (max. L 1.15m) on top of the larger capstone which may have covered gaps. A flat upright slab (0.55m x 0.55m; T 0.2m) crosses the east end of the chamber and further uprights are jammed between it and the NE capstone. These and further uprights to the SW and along the SE sidestone may either be part of the tomb or the field walls extending from the mound.

CL006-157----:
On a generally level area of limestone pavement and rough pasture, on a W-facing slope with reasonable views SW-NW, although inhibited in the foreground by a drystone field boundary, c. 25m to W. Identified in 2017 by Dr Sharon Parr, Scientific Officer of the Burren Programme. It is a roughly rectangular area (3m N-S; 5m E-W) defined by an in situ upright orthostat (H 0.85m; L 2.55m; T 0.08m) which forms a definite E side. Immediately perpendicular to W, a single orthostat (min. H 0.32m; L 0.72m; T 0.06m) has collapsed inwards on the N-side, and may have formed part of a backstone. A flat, possible collapsed orthostat adjacent to W may have formed the western half of the N side. To the immediate S, a series of four parallel orthostats (largest H 0.7m; L 1.16m; T 0.06m) have fallen inwards to E, with the easternmost touching the inside of the large orthostat. It is likely that these four stacked flags formed the western side of the structure. A long, broad earthfast stone (H 0.05m; L 0.88m; T 0.27m) is located to the immediate W. A low drystone wall (max. H 0.4m; L 2.3m; T at top 0.5m; T at base 0.8-0.9m) forms a right-angle to E of the large orthostat, at the N end. It could have been part of a lamb fold/shelter that reused the megalithic structure to one side.

CL008-002001-:
In a slight hollow in an area of limestone pavement, overgrowth and rough pasture, within a large multiperiod field system (CL008-109001-). Marked and labelled 'court cairn' on Robinson's (1977) map. This court tomb (c. 10m N-S; c. 5m E-W) comprises a probable two-chambered gallery accessed from the N through a semicircular court, and surrounded by several overgrown piles of rubble. The access court (int. dims. 4.8m E-W; 4.2m N-S) is open at the N and defined by upright limestone slabs (av. H 1.1m). The N end of the court is obscured by; on the W by an overgrown pile of slabs and on the E by a modern drystone wall. In the centre of the court's S side there is a gap (Wth 0.52m) between two uprights, providing access to the rectangular, N chamber (int. dims. 2.8m N-S; 2m E-W) of the tomb gallery. This is also defined by upright limestone slabs: four sidestones (two at E and two at W), and two uprights at the S. Between these S endstones there is a gap (Wth 0.4m) which may be the entrance to a second chamber to the S, represented by a single E sidestone (L 2.3m). There is an overgrown pile of rubble where this second chamber's W sidestone may have stood, while an E-W running modern wall immediately to the S may have damaged the chamber's S end. There is an enclosure (CL008-002002-) c. 75m to the E.

Additional note, Conn Herriott:
There are currently five recorded court tombs in the Burren, including this monument at Teergonean, three others at Parknabinnia (CL017-180007-), Ballyganner North (CL009-059063-) and Leamaneh North (CL016-020029-), and a possible fifth (CL016-170----) at Ballycasheen. Jones (2003, 188) noted several unusual features in the court tombs at Parknabinnia (CL017-180007-), Ballyganner North (CL009-059063-) and Leamaneh North (CL016-020029-), particularly a narrow, straight-sided forecourt about as wide as the chambers, and a roughly circular or U-shaped cairn, and suggested that these monuments ‘should perhaps be referred to only cautiously as ‘court’ tombs until their relationship to court tombs is better understood.’ Jones (ibid., 193) noted that by contrast with these monuments, the Teergonean court tomb (CL008-002001-) is similar to many northern court tombs with its wider forecourt. However, he (ibid.) also observed that Teergonean court tomb may have had a circular or U-shaped cairn, in common with those at Parknabinnia (CL017-180007-), Ballyganner North (CL009-059063-) and Leamaneh North (CL016-020029-). The details and affinities of the possible court tomb (CL016-170----) at Ballycasheen await further investigation, but it does appear to be set in a low subcircular cairn.
CL008-022----:
Near the top of a gentle SE-facing slope in pasture and within a large multiperiod field system (CL008-109001-). Indicated and labelled 'Dermot & Grania's Bed' on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Listed as 'Megalithic structure site' in the RMP (1996). The OS Name Book (1840) referred to the monument as a 'stone altar' (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 91). According to Borlase (1897, vol. 1, 80) and Westropp (1905, 355), this wedge tomb collapsed in the late 19th century. Both antiquarians described the remains as oriented E-W and embedded or partly embedded in a cairn (already removed). The N and S sidestones (L 3.05m) lay flat, side by side, and each was broken in the centre (Borlase 1897, vol. 1, 80). The original standing height of the tomb chamber was estimated as 1.22m (ibid.). The roof-slab (L 3.05m; Wth 2.49m at W, narrowing to 1.83m at E; T 0.18-0.23m) overlay the N sidestone (Westropp 1905, 355). Under these large prone slabs were found two smaller slabs which were thought to be endstones; because the W endstone (L 1.52m) was longer than that at the E (L 1.22m), Westropp (ibid.) concluded that 'there was the usual eastward taper' (in height and/or width). De Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 91) found no trace of this monument in 1952. During a field inspection in 1998, a trapezoidal area (9m NW-SE; 7m NE-SW at NW side; 5m NE-SW at SE side) that may mark its site was identified; its SW side was defined by a field wall and its other sides consisted of collapsed and grass-covered banks (Wth 1.25m; H 0.2m). The interior was piled with heavily overgrown field-clearance rubble.

CL008-052----:
In a slight hollow on a low prominent hill, in undulating pastureland and outcropping limestone, within a field system (CL008-053001-). Labelled 'Kilmoon Standing Stone' on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. When inspected in 1998, this standing stone (H 3.47m; Wth 0.33m; T 0.15m) was upright, leaned slightly to the E, was uniform in shape along its length and was rectangular in cross-section; it had rough surfaces except where worn smooth by cattle rubbing against it. In 2006 the stone broke at its base and fell to the E. A number of small stones were noted close to it, some of which were well set in the ground while others were lying loose on the ground surface. These could be packing or support stones. The widely visible standing stone may have functioned as a termon marker associated with the medieval church (CL008-049001-) of Kilmoon, which lies 470m to the WSW. Local sources suggest that the standing stone may have marked a route between this church and another church (CL005-108001-) at Killeaney, 1.1km to the NE.

CL009-001013-:
Situated at the E edge of a partially grass-covered limestone plateau, within the NNW sector of an enclosure (CL009-001054-), which lies within a very large multiperiod field system (CL009-001001-/CL005-116---*/CL008-045001*) that stretches from Lissylisheen to Lisdoonvarna. The land falls away to the E, providing good views from NW to S.
This wedge tomb was described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 24) as follows: ‘The monument is very ruined. The chamber is collapsed and the roofstone now lies at the south-east. The south side of the camber is broken and displaced but though the northern sidestone leans heavily inwards, its base appears to be almost in situ. A transverse stone remains in situ at the west end of the chamber. Outer-walling is represented north of the chamber by four stones and on the south by two stones. A single stone at the west indicates a continuation of this feature across the front of the tomb. Beyond it are four stones which may be the remains of a kerb. The grass-covered mound surrounding the structure appears to consist of earth and stones. A stone fence crosses the north end of the mound. The uneven nature of the ground and the distortion cause by the fence makes exact definition of the edge difficult. In general the mound appears to be roughly circular and is approximately 11.50 m. in diameter. It rises to a maximum height of 1.25m near the west end of the chamber.’
While de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) noted that the original dimensions of the chamber could not be ascertained, their plan indicates that it was orientated to the WNW and was c. 2.5m in length and c. 1.7m wide internally at the open W end, narrowing to c. 1m towards the rear. The possible kerb noted is similar to one that was exposed in the excavations of another wedge tomb (CL017-180002-) in Parknabinnia townland (Ó Maoldúin 2015); alternatively, it may be the footing of an outer tomb façade. The mound surrounding the tomb appears to abut it and is therefore possibly of later date. FitzPatrick (2008, 137) suggests that it possibly served as a boundary marker in medieval and later times. The surrounding field system is likely to include settlement elements contemporary with the tomb, similar to those identified in Parknabinnia townland (e.g. CL016-167003-, CL016-173----) (Jones 2008; Jones et al. 2015) and elsewhere on the Burren (e.g. CL006-146----; CL010-230----) (Jones et al. 2011). The well-known cashel of Cahermacnaghten (CL009-001010-) lies c. 340 m to the NW.

CL009-001026-:
On a N-facing slope near the top of a knoll within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-001001-), in an area of rock outcrop and thin grass cover. There is an E–W ravine c. 65m to the S. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 22-3) as a disturbed and partly grass-covered wedge tomb (L c. 2.5m; Wth at rear 1.6m; Wth at front 1.9m) that was embedded in the centre of a mound (12m E–W; 10m N–S; H 1.25m). The tomb appeared to have originally been orientated E–W. A modern N–S drystone field wall crossed the mound and obscured the E end of the chamber. The N and S sides of the tomb seemed to have been made of a single limestone slab set on their long edges; both were broken in two pieces. The E piece of the N sidestone (L 1.4m; min. H 0.75m; T 0.2m) leaned to the N but was probably in situ, the W piece (L 0.8m; H 0.75m; T 0.1m) had been displaced and pointed to the NW. The W fragment (L 1.2m; H 1m; T 0.1m) of the S sidestone pointed to the SW, while the E slab (L 1.6m; min. Wth 0.65m; T 0.1m) had fallen into the chamber. The upper edges of the sidestones sloped down slightly towards the E and were flattened to support the capstone (L 2.5m; Wth 1.9m at W, 1.6m at E; T 0.15m), which rested on the N sidestone slabs and the mound to the S of the chamber. Abutting the W fragment of the N sidestone was an upright slab (L 1.2m; H 0.7m; T 0.1m), orientated SW–NE, which may have closed the W end of the chamber. A slab (L 1.2m; H 0.65m) set in the field wall to the SE of the chamber possibly indicated the remains of an outer wall. An inspection of the tomb in 1998 found it unaltered in the interim (SMR file).
There is a cashel (CL009-001025-) c. 15m to the S. This is one of multiple cases in the Burren of cashels being built adjacent to or over Early Bronze Age ritual structures, as at Creevagh (CL010-095002-) (Comber 2008, 106-8) and Caherconnell (CL009-030011-) (Hull and Comber 2008, 123-30), and perhaps also in the case of another wedge tomb (CL009-001013-) in Lissylisheen, c. 1.37km to the NW. This fits into a widespread medieval phenomenon of utilising prehistoric landmarks in order to emphasise important land divisions and nodes (FitzPatrick 2008, 137; Jones and Comber 2008, 162).

CL009-013007-:
On level ground in pasture within a multiperiod field system (CL009-013001-), with wide views of the surrounding plateau. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 25-6) as a disturbed, E–W orientated wedge tomb (exposed L 2m; Wth at rear 0.9m; Wth at front 1.05m; exposed H at rear 0.2m; exposed H at front 0.3m) in the centre of a grass-covered mound (est. diam. c. 13m; H c. 1.8m) which had been damaged by later activities. A stone (H 0.4m; L 0.4m) at the SE of the mound may have indicated the original extent of the cairn. In the centre of the mound the upper parts of the tomb chamber’s N and S sidestones were exposed; each consisted of a single limestone slab, similar in size (visible L 1.9–2m; H 0.3m at W, 0.2m at E; T 0.1–0.15m) and with flat top edges sloping evenly from W to E. Their E ends were buried in the mound. Two smaller slabs (L 0.4–0.5m; H 0.1; T 0.1–0.15m) standing to the NE and SW of the chamber were probably remnants of a wall surrounding the tomb at a distance of c. 0.4m. An inspection in 1998 found it unaltered in the interim.

CL009-019----:
On a low ridge in an area of grass and scrub cover on a plateau, with land sloping gently to E.  Westropp (1899, 370) recorded marks of fire on this monument. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 20) as an E–W orientated wedge tomb (L c. 5m; Wth at rear 1.75m; Wth at front 2.5m; H at rear 1.35m; H at front c. 1.6m) in the centre of a grass-covered mound (c. 12m E–W; c. 9m N–S; est. H c. 1.5m). The sides of the chamber were each formed by a single limestone slab (L 5-5.15m; H 1.35-1.4m; T 0.25m) with flat dressed upper edges sloping up to the W. The S sidestone (L 5m; H 1.35m; T 0.25m) was mostly intact. The E portion of the N sidestone (L 2.3m; H 1.3–1.35m; T 0.25m) was still standing; the W portion (L 2.75m; Wth 1.4m) was broken and lay prone to the N. The back of the chamber was closed by two low slabs (N stone: L 0.75m; H 0.3m; T 0.15m; S stone: L 0.9m; H 0.25m; T 0.2m) standing on edge. These may be the remains of a single slab, of which a possible fragment (L 1.5m; T 0.2m) lay to the E. A collapsed capstone (3.45m E–W; 1.75m N–S) rested against the internal side of the N sidestone and two more slabs (W fragment: L 2.3m; E fragment: L 1.6m) lying on the capstone may have been part of it. Two smaller slabs (L 0.7m; H 0.3-0.4m; T 0.12-0.15m) stood upright W of the N and S sidestones. They were set perpendicular to the line of the chamber and may have emphasised the entrance. A field wall, marking the townland boundary between Baur North and Cregavockoge, runs N–S over the W end of the tomb chamber. An inspection in 1998 found the wedge tomb unaltered in the interim (SMR file). A cist (CL009-019002-) lies c. 24m to the NE.

CL009-020001-:
On a SE-facing slope, at the edge of a plateau overlooking the W end of the Kilcorney valley, in an area of grass and hazel within a multiperiod field system (CL009-255----). Labelled ‘Dermot and Grania’s Bed’ on the 1920 ed. of the OS 6-inch map. This wedge tomb was described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 20-21) as being well preserved but of unusual construction, as set within the E end of the chamber (L 2.35m; Wth at W 1.4m narrowing to 1.15m at E; H at W 1m) was another smaller structure (max. L 1.45m; H 0.8m). This resulted in a doubling of the N and S sidestones at the E end of the tomb and the roof. Immediately outside the S sidestone two stones were set in a line with a third set more to the W of these. Four stones along the N side of the chamber may have been the remains of outer walling. Access to the tomb was gained between two groups of three stones, each group set transversely across the W ends of the N and S sidestones. The tomb was set in the centre of an irregular grass-covered mound (c. 12m E–W; c. 8.5m N–S), which was disturbed on the N side. A field visit in 1998 found that, other than increased hazel encroachment from the N, the tomb was unaltered (SMR file). Westropp (1899, 370) offers several comparisons for the inner structure, including another wedge tomb (CL036-034----) in east Clare. More recently, Grant (2010, 47) has suggested that the inner chamber was a cist added after the original construction of the tomb. Several human bones recovered from the latter chamber appear to belong to a young adult (ibid., 46). One of these bones was radiocarbon-dated to 2033–1897 BC (ibid., 2009, 5; 2010, 47), which is relatively late in the typical range of wedge tomb use (Brindley and Lanting 1992). There are three cairns nearby: one (CL009-020002-) c. 50m to S, another (CL009-145----) c. 150m to ENE and a third (CL009-145003-) c. 160m to ESE.

CL009-021012-:
On a gentle S-facing slope of a plateau, within a multiperiod field system (CL009-021001-), with good views from NE to SW. This monument appears to be the remains of a very poorly preserved unclassified megalithic tomb. A possible chamber is defined by two upright slabs on its N side with two prostrate slabs to the S. The chamber is aligned NE-SW. It occupies the NE end of an associated cairn (11.3m NE-SW; 7.4m NW-SE) that was probably originally circular or oval-shaped in plan. The cairn survives from S to W to N but there is little or no trace of it from N to E, and particularly so from E to S. It is retained by a distinctive double kerb (Wth 1.2m; H 0.8-0.9m). The inner kerb is partly defined by very large kerbstones (H 1.2-1.4m) set upright and rising above general height of the kerb itself. On the outer kerb, horizontally laid stones, two courses high, are visible at SW. Some of the cairn material has spilled outside the kerb.
A possible cist (CL009-0021059-) is visible to the S of the chamber and to its SW there is a possible stone circle (CL009-021060-). Both of these features suggest that the megalithic tomb was subsequently reused.

On a plateau, within a multiperiod field system (CL009-255---), immediately to the W of a N-S running laneway that leads to a farmhouse to the N. Indicated on Robinson’s map (1977). The internal height of the chamber increases from W (H 0.86m) to E and it is covered neatly by a capstone. CL009-034001-:
Situated on bare limestone pavement within sight of the main N-S routeway through the high Burren region and c. 7.5km S of Ballyvaughan village. The portal tomb at Poulnabrone (Poll na Brón or ‘hollow of the millstone’), perhaps one of Ireland’s best-known megalithic tombs, is one of some 184 portal tombs whose distribution is concentrated in the N third of the country and in the SE counties of Leinster.
Poulnabrone comprises a single rectilinear chamber (aligned NNE-SSW; L 2.8m; Wth 1.2m between the portals, c. 1.4m across the centre narrowing again to 1.1m at the backstone) with an entrance defined by two tall portal stones. The portal stones were set with their long axes parallel to the chamber. The E portal is a blocky pillar stone (H 1.75m; L 0.63m; T 0.25m) which was replaced following excavation as it had a number of horizontal and vertical cracks. The W portal stone (H 1.43m; L 1.2m; T 0.07-0.2m) narrows towards the base. A transverse slab or sillstone (L 0.87m; T 0.09-0.12m) is set on edge between the portals and the back of the chamber is formed by a backstone (L 2.1m; H 0.43m; T 0.2-0.35m). The W side is formed by a single sidestone (L 1.62m; max. H 0.38m; T 0.13m), leaning inwards at an angle of 70 degrees. The E side is defined by two sidestones. The N one (H 1.28m; L 1.3m; T 0.13-0.2m) leans inwards slightly and the S one (max. H 0.8m; L 1.1-1.2m; T 0.05-0.12m), also leaning slightly inwards, is set outside the N one and overlapping it by 0.2m. A large trapezoidal roofstone (L 3.7m; Wth 2.85m over the entrance narrowing to 1.55m at the rear) oversails the entrance and slopes downwards towards the backstone. It comprises a complete clint block prised from the surrounding pavement. Partially overlying the backstone and resting on the cairn is a large flat slab (L 1.8m N-S; Wth 1.75m; T c. 0.15-0.23m) which is likely to have served as a subsidiary roofstone. The tomb is surrounded by a low mound or cairn, roughly oval in shape (c. 10.5m N-S; max. 8.6m E-W; H 0.7-0.9m).
The chamber and sections of the surrounding cairn were excavated in 1986-8 (licence no. E000351) as part of a major conservation project (Lynch 2014, 1). The excavation revealed that the orthostats of the chamber sit directly on the limestone pavement, with the single large roofstone helping to hold them in position. The surrounding low cairn of stones (of simple construction, comprising limestone slabs and smaller stones with no formal kerb) provided lateral support and a low sillstone marked the entrance to the chamber. It is unclear if the small, cist-like feature (referred to as a portico) constructed at the entrance to the chamber is an original feature or a later Bronze Age construction. At least 0.25m of calcareous soil covered the area at the time the tomb was built.
The commingled unburnt remains of at least 35 individuals were recovered from the chamber, ranging in date from c. 3800 cal BC to c. 3200 cal BC. The earliest burials are likely to date to the time of the construction of the tomb which would place it at the very beginning of the Irish Neolithic. …
CL009-046----:
Near the top of a S-facing slope in rough pasture, with wide views to the S and W. Indicated on Robinson’s map (1977). Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 24) as a S-facing wedge tomb (L c. 2.5m; Wth at rear 1.65m; Wth at front 1.75m) embedded in the centre of a broken and uneven mound (11m N–S; c. 10m E–W; H 0.6m). A modern N–S drystone field wall extended along the E side of the mound. The tomb was constructed from very coarse limestone slabs. The E and W sides each comprised a single upright limestone slab set on its long edge. The E sidestone (L 2.8m; max. H at N 1.2m; T c. 0.3m) leaned to the W, and its top edge was flaked and uneven. The W sidestone (L 2.85m; H at S 1.2m; H at N 1.05m; T 0.2–0.5m) had a thin and concave top edge. Continuing the line of the W sidestone to the N, there was another block (L 1.4m; H 0.4m; T 0.2m) which may not have been in situ. The S end of the chamber appeared to be partly disturbed, with a stone (L 1.7m; H 0.35m; T 0.2m) set upright on its long edge, extending from the E sidestone to perhaps beyond the W sidestone. Parallel to and S of this stone there were two upright slabs, ‘possibly displaced doorstones’ (ibid.). The more northerly of these (L 1.3m; H 0.8m; T 0.15m) leaned to the N. The second one (L 1.9m; H 0.9m; T c. 0.15m) leaned to the S and was ‘well set’ (ibid.). Within the chamber there were two slabs, both oriented E–W across the width of the tomb: the N stone (L 1.4m; Wth c. 0.6m) lay flat, while the S stone (L 1.05m; H c. 0.25m; T c. 0.3m) was firmly set upright on its long edge but was considered by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) not to be in situ. An inspection of the tomb in 1998 found it unaltered in the interim (SMR file). Another wedge tomb (CL009-048001-) lies c. 350m to the S.

CL009-048001-:
On a hillock at the N end of the Carran depression in an area of reclaimed pastureland and cragland. Indicated and labelled ‘Cromlech’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 24–5) as a much collapsed and greatly disturbed wedge tomb (est. int. dims. L c. 2.65m; Wth at rear 1.65m; Wth at front 1.75m), aligned SW–NE, which was embedded in the NW sector of a subcircular mound (diam. c. 6m). A NNW-SSE running field wall crossed the W part it.
The N side of the chamber was originally defined by an upright limestone slab (L c. 2.65m; H at E c. 1.3; H at W c. 1.35m; T 0.2–0.25m), now broken. The base remained in situ, in three pieces, and the upper part of the stone was in two pieces to the N of the base. The S side was defined by two upright slabs, which may have originally formed a single sidestone. The E slab (L 1m; H 0.8m) appeared to have been slightly displaced. The W slab (L 1.25m; H 1.1m) leaned to the N and under it there was a stone (H 0.2m) that was probably not in its original position. The capstone (L 4.5m; Wth at NE 2.4m; Wth at SW 2.7m; T 0.25m) had slid to the N and overlay the N sidestone. It was also supported by the more westerly of the S sidestones and by a boulder (H 0.5m) at its E end; the latter did not appear to be an original feature. The capstone was in this position when described by Westropp (1898, 366). Clear indications of the mound surrounding the chamber survived to the E and S of the tomb.
An inspection of the tomb in 1998 found it to have been slightly damaged in the interim (SMR file). The site of a cairn (CL009-048002-) lies c. 44m to the SE. Another wedge tomb (CL009-046----) lies c. 350m to the N.
