CL009-059063-:
On a rise in the floor of a wide valley in rough pasture and limestone pavement, a N-S ravine immediately to the W. Within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-059001-). Indicated and labelled ‘Cromlech’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 29-31; see attachment) as a damaged and partly covered court cairn (7.5m NNE-SSW; 2.2-2.7m WNW-ESE; max. H c. 1.1m) embedded in a poorly defined mound on a low natural knoll. The tomb was oriented NNE-SSW and comprised a two-chambered gallery accessed from the NNE through a narrow court. The court (L c. 2m; Wth c. 2.2m) was open at the N, and lined at the E and W by low rows of upright limestone slabs. The E row (L 2.6m) included five slabs (L 0.5-0.9m; H 0.25-0.45m; T 0.35m). The W row (L 2.1m) was composed of two in situ slabs (L 0.7-1m; Wth 0.5-0.6m; T 0.05-0.1m) which were incorporated in an overlying field boundary, as well as two slabs to the W which were more disturbed.
At the S end of the court, the gallery (4.2m NNE-SSW; 2.5-2.7m WNW-ESE; max. H c. 1.1m) was accessed through an entrance (Wth c. 0.95m) defined by two tall jambs. The E jamb (H 1.25m; Wth 0.5m; T 0.4m) is split longitudinally. The W jamb (H 1.6m; Wth 0.4m; T 0.35m) appeared to be one of a pair. Immediately to the N was the in situ base of its broken N partner (original H 1.65), most of which lay E-W in front of the gallery entrance. A low flat threshold slab (L c. 0.85m; max. Wth c. 0.45m) appeared to perhaps not be original.
The gallery’s N chamber (1.5m NNE-SSW; 1.8m WNW-ESE) had a single outward-leaning E sidestone (L 1.5m; H 1.05m; T 0.1-0.15m) with an uneven top edge that sloped sharply to the N. The W sidestone (L 1.2m; H 1.4m; T 0.2m) did not reach the SW corner of the chamber; this gap (L 0.4m) may originally have been covered by a disturbed overlapping sidestone (L 1.15; H 0.95m; T 0.15m) to the W. Another upright slab (L 1.15m; H 0.6m; T 0.15m) of unclear function was also set to the W of the chamber. A modern N–S drystone field-wall obscured part of the chamber’s W side. The N chamber was separated from the S by two pillar-like jambs (H 1m; Wth 0.35-0.4m; T 0.25-0.3m) set (1m apart) adjacent to the E and W walls. A threshold-like stone (L 1.6m; Wth 0.6m; T 0.2m) lying E-W across the gallery between the jambs was thought to be a lintel, fallen from over this accessway between the gallery chambers (see also Westropp 1897, 119).
The S chamber (2.25m NNE-SSW; 1.7m ESE-WNW) had a large sidestone on either side. That at E (L 2.7m; H 1m; T 0.2-0.4m) had a broken and uneven top edge, sloping to S. Outside this sidestone to the E were several lower upright slabs (max. H 0.25m) which seemed to be packing stones. The W sidestone (L 2.45m; H 0.75m; T 0.15-0.2m) had a rough, uneven top edge. Its S end was concealed by a later E-W field boundary which abutted the tomb’s SW corner, but a gap (L 0.4m) was visible between this sidestone and the SW corner of the gallery. As in the N chamber, the gap was covered by a parallel outer slab (L 1.45m; H 0.9m; T 0.1m), to the N of which was another slab (L 1.2m; H 1.1m; T 0.1m). These were thought to likely be high-pitched slab corbels. …
CL009-059069-:
At the W edge of a W-sloping limestone pavement, with a hazel wood to the W. Within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-059001-). Indicated and labelled ‘Cromlech’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 31-2; see attachment) as a very disturbed wedge tomb (est. L 2.8m), oriented E-W and embedded in the centre of a mound. Only the N sidestone of the tomb was intact, and the extent of the mound could not be traced. The N sidestone was an upright limestone slab (L 2.85m; H at W 1.37m; H at E 0.8m; T 0.1-0.2m) set on its long edge. The straight top edge was dressed, sloping down evenly from W to E. The E and W edges were almost vertical. A block (L 0.85m; H 0.3m; T 0.3m) to the N of the sidestone at its E end was considered a possible packing-stone. To the S of the sidestone (1.2m away) lay the fallen capstone (L 3.2m; Wth at W 1.7m; Wth at E 1.25m; T 0.12m), oriented E-W. The W to E slope of the top edge of the N sidestone and greater width of the capstone at the W indicated that—as is typical among wedge tombs—the chamber was wider and higher at the W.
The capstone overlay several slab fragments, including two large pieces (each L 1.6m; Wth 1-1.1m; T 0.1m) which may have been part of the displaced S sidestone. The S edge of the E fragment was straight (L 1.15m) and dressed, suggesting that it was part of the S sidestone’s top edge. Between the N sidestone and S sidestone fragments lay two slabs of unclear function. To the W of these were two small upright slabs (L 0.3-0.4m; H 0.2m), aligned N-S, which may have formed part of the W end of the tomb. A stone (L 0.5m; H 0.2m; T 0.1m) standing on edge 1m to the S of the capstone may have been part of the outer wall of the tomb.
An inspection in 1997 found the tomb to be unaltered, although with more briars growing up around it. A possible megalithic structure (CL009-059068-) lies c. 202m to the N.

CL009-059072-:
Near the top of a W-facing slope, which becomes steeper immediately to W. In pasture within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-059001-). Indicated and labelled ‘Cromlech’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 33-4; see attachment) as a large and well-preserved wedge tomb (L c. 4.2m; Wth at SW 2.95m, narrowing to 2m at NE; H at SW 1.6m, dropping to 1m at NE) that was embedded in the centre of a low circular mound (diam. c. 14.5m; H not discernible). The trapezoidal tomb was oriented SW-NE. A modern NW–SE drystone field wall crossed the mound, incorporating the W side of the tomb. Each side of the tomb comprised a limestone slab standing on its long edge, with top edge flattened to support a capstone. The NW sidestone (L 5.4m; H at SW 1.6m; H at NE 1m; T 0.2-0.25m) was also worked on the inside and outside of its top edge. The upper part of the SE sidestone (L at top 5.8m; L at base 5.45m; H at SW 1.7m; H at NE 1m; T 0.25-0.3m) jutted out at its SW end. The NE endstone (L at base 1.95m; H 1m; T 0.15-0.2m) fitted neatly between the sidestones, and its S top corner was broken (L 0.3m; H 0.4m). The SW end was mostly blocked by a slab (L 2.4m; H 1.6m; T 0.2m), the side edges of which were also finely dressed. Between this endstone (‘blocking stone’ [ibid.]) and the NW sidestone there was a gap (L 0.6m), its lower part covered by a second, overlapping endstone (‘doorstone’ [ibid.]) (L 0.95; H 0.4m; T 0.15). The top edge of this slab appeared broken, supporting Westropp’s (1909, 18) proposal that it may have originally also covered the upper part of the gap at this end of the tomb. De Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 33) suggested that one of the slab fragments found outside the same end of the tomb may have been part of this broken endstone. Other fragments inside and outside the chamber appeared to be part of the broken capstone (est. L c. 6.1m; Wth 4.2m), two large pieces of which (L c. 2.8m; Wth c. 2-2.5m; T 0.25-0.3m) were still in position resting on the W and SW corners. (Westropp (1909, 18) described ‘small basins’/‘cup marks’ on the upper face of the fallen capstone fragments within the chamber.) Two slabs (L 0.4m; H 0.15m; T 0.1m) were set into the ground 1-2m to the W of the W corner of the tomb.
An inspection of the tomb in 1997 found it unaltered, except that the roof had been repaired by the Office of Public Works. The precariously balanced capstone fragments had collapsed into the chamber and were put back in place, with a steel bar supporting their NE edges.
A hut site (CL009-251----) lies c. 80m to the NNW, a cashel (CL009-059071-) lies c. 85m to the S and an enclosure (CL009-059074-) lies c. 109m to the ENE.

CL009-059077-:
On a slight rise on a S-facing slope overlooking an E-W valley, in rough pasture within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-059001-). Situated at the NW edge and highest point of a cashel interior (CL009-059076-).  Indicated and named ‘Cromlech’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 32; attached) as a large wedge tomb chamber (L c. 4.25m; Wth at W 2m, narrowing to 1.45m at E centre; min. H at W c. 1.5m, dropping to c. 1.15m at E), its W end covered by spill from the cashel wall. There were some traces of a mound surrounding the chamber, which was oriented E-W and comprised a single large sidestone at S, two overlapping sidestones at N, and a broken capstone which had collapsed into the chamber. The S sidestone (L 4.3m; H 1.65m at W, 1m at E; T 0.2-0.3m) had a straight and roughly dressed top edge, sloping W-E. The vertical W edge was also worked. Of the two N sidestones, that at W (L 3m; H 1.35m at W, 1.15m at E; T 0.2m) had a dressed top edge and its E end was broken. The E slab at N (L 1.9m; max. H 1.35m; est. T c. 0.15m) overlapped (L 0.25m) the N side of the W slab. Most of its top edge (L 1m) was dressed. The vertical W end was also worked, and the E end bore chipping marks. Because this slab was oriented more WNW-ESE, de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) thought it may have been a later addition. The capstone had split roughly down the middle, and was in five pieces (L 1.2-3m; T 0.15-0.2m) within the chamber: two leaning against the N sidestones, and three against the S.
De Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) followed Westropp (1901, 290) in describing a low souterrain which extended W from the W end of the chamber into the cashel wall however, an inspection of the tomb in 1997 found no evidence for a souterrain.
This is an example of a cashel being built adjacent to or over an Early Bronze Age ritual structure. Other examples are known in the Burren including Creevagh (CL010-095002-) (Comber 2008, 106-8) and Caherconnell (CL009-030011-) (Hull and Comber 2008, 123-30), as well as two in Lissylisheen (CL009-001026- and CL009-001013-).

CL009-059086-:
On a gentle SW-facing slope in rough pasture within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-059001-). Indicated and named ‘Cromlech’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 32-3; attacahed) as a well-preserved, E-W-oriented trapezoidal wedge tomb (L 2.75m; Wth at W 1.75m, narrowing to 1.35m at E; H at W 1.95m, dropping to 1.3m at E) embedded in the centre of a grass-covered oval mound (c. 12m E-W; c. 10m N-S; est. H c. 1.2m). A stone (L 0.9m; H 0.4m) was set upright on its long edge (aligned NW-SE) in the NW part of the mound.
The tomb chamber comprised single limestone slabs at each side, with dressed top edges supporting a capstone (L 4m; Wth at W 2.5m, Wth at E 2m; T 0.15-0.2m). On the upper face of the latter Westropp (1901, 291) had noted two ‘curious channels, but manifestly water-worn, probably ages before the block was raised’. The N sidestone (L 3.7m; H at W 1.9m, H at E 1.3m; T 0.2-0.3m) had a vertical crack running through its W centre. The top edge of the S sidestone (L 4.1m; H at W 1.6m, H at E 1.25m; T 0.2-0.25m) was broken near the W end by a natural cavity (D 0.4m). Only the base of the E endstone survived (L 1.1m; extant H 0.35m; T 0.15m), its top obscured by a drystone wall. There was a 0.12m gap between this slab and the N sidestone, although de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) suggested that this endstone may have originally closed the entire E end of the chamber. The slab at the W end of the chamber (H 1.95; L 1.1m; T 0.15m) abutted the N sidestone, and had a straight S edge. There was a 0.65m gap between this endstone and the S sidestone. The top N corner of this endstone was broken, relatively recently in de Valera and Ó Nualláin’s (ibid.) view. The interior of the chamber was lower (D c. 0.5m) and undulating. At least three slabs (Wth 0.25-0.5m) were laid flat near the W end, and perhaps another near the E. An inspection of the tomb in 1997 found it unaltered.

CL009-059092-:
On a broad high point, in briars and rough pasture within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-059001-). This wedge tomb (int. dims. 4.4m E-W; 1.65m N-S at E; 1.5m N-S at W) is oriented E-W, and comprises a rectangular chamber of limestone slabs (av. T c. 0.1m): two sidestones at both N and S, an endstone at W, a possible ex situ endstone at E, and two collapsed capstone fragments within the chamber. The W sidestone at S (L 2.45m; H 1m) is the largest. The E sidestone at S (L 1.1; H 1.1m) is out of line with this larger slab, being set 0.3m to the S. The N sidestones (L 1.2-1.4m; H 0.3-0.8m; T 0.1-0.2) are in alignment, but there is a 1.8m gap between them, from which perhaps another slab was removed. The W endstone (L 1.8m; H 1.2m) is in position. The E endstone appears to have fallen outward: there is a flat-lying slab (L 2m; Wth 1m) 1m to the E of the chamber, oriented N-S. Of the two capstone fragments in the chamber, one (L 2m; Wth 0.9m) lies prone in the W while the other (L 1.4m) partly rests on the top edge of the large S sidestone.
The wedge tomb is integrated into a field wall running NW-SE, c. 3.5m to the SE of a junction with another wall running NE-SW. An enclosure (CL009-059116-) lies c. 28m to the NE.

CL009-059093-:
On a SE-facing slope in pasture and hazel scrub, within a multiperiod field system (CL009-059001-). Listed as ‘Cist’ in the RMP (1996), following de Valera and Ó Nualláin’s (1961, 43; see attached) interpretation of the monument as a divided/double cist, probably influenced by ‘true megalithic chambers’. A small wedge tomb (L 3.4m; Wth at WSW 0.9m, narrowing to 0.8m at ENE; max. H 0.8m) embedded in the centre of a grass-covered oval mound (c. 5m ENE-WSW; c. 3m NNW-SSE; H c. 1m). The tomb chamber comprises two parallel ENE-WSW rows of limestone slabs (0.9m apart at W, 0.8m apart at E), set upright on their long edges. There are two stones on the N side (W stone L 1.3m; H 0.3m; T 0.1m; E stone L 1.4m; H 0.6m; T 0.2m), with a 0.2m gap between them. There are four stones on the S side, three of which are set close together (W stone L 0.6m; H 0.1m; T 0.1m; central stone L 0.15m; Wth 0.1m; H 0.1m; E stone L 1.25m; H 0.2m; T 0.05m). A fourth coaligned slab lies c. 0.75m to the WSW. A transverse slab (L 0.7m; H 0.25m; T 0.1m) was set upright on its long edge across the chamber (i.e., oriented NNW-SSE), 0.8m from the ENE end. The possible continuation of the tomb in that direction may have been damaged by a NNW-SSE field bank.
A wedge tomb (CL009-059094-) lies c. 13m to the SW and another wedge tomb (CL009-162----) lies c. 15m to N.

CL009-059094-:
On a gentle SW-facing slope in pasture in a clearing in hazel woodland, with wide views from S to W, and within a multiperiod field system (CL016-020028-). Indicated and labelled ‘Dermot & Grania’s Bed’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 42-3; link below) as a largely intact wedge tomb (L c. 4.5m; Wth at W 2.1m, narrowing to 1.1m at E; H at W 1.6m, dropping to 1.45m at E) that was partly embedded in an elongated suboval mound (12m E-W; 8m N-S; H 0.7m), the edges of which were difficult to define at N and E. Of the kerbing noted by Westropp (1913, 257) that girded the mound, only one possible kerbstone (L 0.75m; H 0.2m) was identified at its SW edge. A field wall, running N-S, crossed the E end of the chamber.
Both sides of the chamber, which was trapezoidal in plan and orientated WSW-ENE, comprised a massive limestone slab standing on its long edge. The S sidestone (L 5.05m; H at W 1.65m; H at E 1.25m; T 0.15-0.25m) was intact but had a central vertical crack. Its straight top edge was hammer dressed and sloped evenly from W to E. Westropp (ibid.) noted that a small hole was pierced through it. The N sidestone (L c. 4.55m) was broken and part of its central section was missing. The two upstanding portions included one to the W (L 0.9m; H 1.65m; T 0.1-0.2m) and one to the E (L 2.5m; H 1.5m; T 0.1-0.25m), with the base (L 0.35m; H 0.15m; T 0.12m) of the broken section in between them. The top edge of E stone was also hammer dressed. The E end of the tomb was open but what appeared to be a displaced backstone (L 1.75m; H 1m; T 0.12m) was situated at the E end of the N sidestone and leaned to the S. Parts of the edges of this stone appeared to be hammer dressed and the top W corner was chipped leaving a gap (L 0.6m; H 0.8m) with a curved edge. The entrance opened to the W and near the W end of the N sidestone, an upright stone (L 0.7m; H 0.35m; T 0.15m), oriented NE-SW, may have been part of an entry feature. The enormous capstone (L 5.5m; Wth at W 2.85m, narrowing to 2.35m at E; T 0.2-0.3m) was broken in two, with a piece missing to the N of a central fracture. It rested on the sidestones and the top it was covered by a low pile of earth and stone.
Outer walling was visible to the S and N of the sidestones and also to the W of the entrance. The surviving portion of the outer S wall (min. L 3.9m) comprised three in situ upright slabs (L 0.35-0.85m; H 0.05-0.15m; T 0.05-0.1m) with a gap (L 1.6m) between the W and central slabs. A fourth slab (L 0.5m; H 0.7m; T 0.2m) set in the N-S field boundary, 0.5m to E, was also though to be part of this wall. Three slabs of the outer N wall (L c. 5.5m) also survived in situ and comprised a slab (L 1.65m; erect H 1.8; T 0.12-0.2m) leaning over at the W end of the tomb, another slab (L 0.9m; H 0.5m; T 0.1m) set 1.45m to its E and a third slab (L 1.25m; H 0.55m; T 0.1-0.15m) at the E end of the tomb. A slab (L 0.85m; H 0.2m; T 0.1m) situated 0.7m further to the E may also have been related to this wall. A slab (L 1.2m; H 0.3m; T 0.15m) between this wall and the N sidestone may have indicated a doubling of this outer walling. …

CL009-067----:
Near the top of a gentle S-facing slope in an area of rough pasture and exposed limestone pavement, with wide views from E to W, and within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-032001-). Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 26-7; link below) as a wedge tomb (L c. 2.6m; Wth at W 1.4m, narrowing to 1.2m at E; H at W 1.2m, dropping to 0.75m at E) with very faint traces of a surrounding mound. The subrectangular chamber was oriented SW-NE. Both of its long sidestones consisted of single limestone slabs (N sidestone L 3.1m; H at W 1.6m, dropping to 0.85m at E; T 0.2m; S sidestone L 2.6m; H at W 1.1m, dropping to 1.05m at E; T 0.1-0.2m); their top edges were hammer dressed. A broken slab (L 0.75m; extant H 0.45m; T 0.1m) extending to the S, from near the W end of the N sidestone, may have been a sill or doorstone. There was a gap (L 0.6m) between it and the S sidestone. The E end of the chamber was open, but 0.8m to the NE of the N sidestone, an upright slab (L 0.65m; H 0.25m; T 0.06m), also oriented SW-NE, was possibly indicative of a continuation of the chamber or a separate end-chamber. Four stones (L 1.4-2.05m; T 0.1m) found resting on and against the sidestones, and prostrate inside and outside the chamber were probably fragments of the capstone.
The chamber was surrounding by outer walling on all sides. That on the N side (L c. 7.5m) consisted of eight near-contiguous or overlapping slabs (L 0.4-1.4m; H 0.25-1.4m; T 0.05-0.2m), set 0.5-1m outside the chamber. The function of two further upright stones (H 0.15-0.4m) at its W end was unclear. On the S side, the walling comprised four upright slabs: two (L 0.6-1.1m; H 0.15-0.4m) at the W end and two (L 1.2-1.3m; H 1.15-1.6m) at the E, with a gap (L c. 3m) between them in which a slab (L 1.6m) lay flat. The most westerly stone was covered by a loose prostrate slab (L 2m) and another prostrate slab (L 0.65m; H 0.8m) lay to the E of the second slab. (One of these had apparently been upright and part of the walling when the monument was visited by Westropp (1901, 286).) The E end consisted of a single slab (L 1.4m; H 0.1m) and at least two slabs formed the W side, one (L 1.75m; H 0.9m) with a seemingly quite fresh vertical crack in it. Extending to the E from the S end of this slab was another slab (L 1.15m; H 0.6m) which may have been displaced. An inspection of the tomb in May 1997 found it to be unaltered in the interim. A cashel (CL009-064001-) lies c. 76m to the NW.

CL009-084006-:
On a plateau with wide views, especially from S to W, and within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-084001-). Indicated and labelled ‘Standing Stone’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Listed at ‘Standing stone’ in the RMP (1996). This stone row (L 6.5m) comprises three limestone slabs set upright in a gryke and oriented NNE-SSW. The N stone (H 1.15m; Wth 1m; T 0.1m) has a rounded pointed top. Situated 1.7m to its SSW, the central stone (H 1.67m; Wth 1.4m; T 0.15m) is highest towards its N end. The flat-topped S stone (H 0.6m; Wth 1.2m; T 0.1m-0.15m) is 1.2m SSW of the central one. Coffey (1990, 61) suggested that these stones originally formed part of an ancient wall and that most of its stones were removed to build ‘a more modern wall close by’.

CL009-084007-:
Near the W edge of a plateau, in rough pasture, overlooking hazel-covered craglands to the S and W; within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-084001-). Indicated on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map and named ‘Cromlechs’ on the latter ed. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 27-8 – see link below) as a large partly collapsed wedge tomb (L c. 4.75m; Wth at W 2.1m, narrowing to 0.8m at E; H at W 1.4m, dropping to 0.65m at E) divided into two chambers. The tomb is embedded in the E end of an irregular low elongated mound (c. 20.5m ENE-WSW; c. 4.8-8.5m NNW-SSE; H c. 0.5-0.8m). An unclassified megalithic tomb (CL009-084008-) and a possible cist (CL009-084009-), which appear to have been subsequently added, occupy its W end.
The wedge tomb, trapezoidal in plan, is oriented WSW-ENE. A number of the edges and tops of its stones are dressed. The N and S sides of the larger W chamber (L 2.85m; Wth at W 2.1 narrowing to 1.65m at E; H at W 1.4m; 0.8m at E) consist of a single limestone slab. The N sidestone (L 3.25m; T 0.2-0.25m) had collapsed inward, if erect it would have stood 1.2m high at the W end and 0.9m at the E. The S sidestone (L 4.35m; H at W 1.4m; H at E 0.8m; T 0.2-0.25m) is massive and its E end forms part of the S wall of the S side of the smaller E chamber (L 1.9m; Wth at W 1.6, narrowing to 0.8m at E; H at W 0.8m; 0.65m at E). Another slab (L 1.3m; H 0.8m; T 0.15m) completes this side of the latter chamber. The N side is also constructed of two slabs (W slab L 0.8; H 0.85m; T 0.15-0.2m; E slab L 1.3m; H 0.7m; T 0.15m) that are not quite in line with the N side of the W chamber. The chambers are divided by a segmental slab (L 1.5m; H 1m). Part of the roofstone (L 3.15m; Wth at W 3m narrowing to 2.3m at E; T 0.15-0.25m) still caps the tomb. A broken fragment of it (L 1.35m; Wth 3.05m; T 0.15-0.25m) lies on the ground immediately to the W. The W chamber is partially closed by a slab (L 1.4m; H 1.05m; T 0.1m) set 0.4m inside it. Two other stones are lying on the ground to the W of its N sidestone.
Traces of outer walling survive on both sides of the tomb. That on the S side (L c. 7.3m) consists of five in situ upright slabs, two recumbent slabs and a slab leaning against the most easterly upright slab. On the N side, only two slabs (L c. 3.8m) survive, 1.8m apart. To the N of the more easterly of these stones, two further parallel slabs suggest ‘some doubling of the outer walling’ (ibid., 28). CL009-084008-:
Within the W half of a low elongated mound (c. 20.5m ENE-WSW; c. 4.8-8.5m NNW-SSE; H c. 0.5-0.8m) associated with a wedge tomb (CL009-084007-) that lies c. 2.5m to the NE; a possible cist (CL009-084009-) lies c. 2.5m to the SW. Indicated on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map and labelled ‘Cromlechs’ on the latter ed. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 28-9) as a completely collapsed structure that was difficult to interpret. It is defined by a roofstone (L 2.55m; Wth 2m; T 0.15m), oriented roughly NE-SW, and almost all the other structural elements are concealed beneath it. A large slab (L 2.1m; Wth 1.05m; T 0.1-0.15m) visible under the S edge of the roofstone may be the collapsed S sidestone; its straight S edge may have supported the roofstone when it was upright. An erect stone (L 0.9m; H 0.75m; T 0.1-0.15m), N of this slab, may mark the E end of the chamber. A set stone (L 1.4m; H 0.45m; T 0.1m) to its E and a second slab may define its N side. The function of a displaced prostrate slab (L 0.9m) at the SW corner of the roofstone could not be determined. The mound associated with the wedge tomb narrows to the E of this structure, which suggested to de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid., 29) that the original mound had been extended to incorporate it and the possible cist to its W. On the basis of the proportions of the slabs of this structure, de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) concluded that it was best regarded as a small megalithic chamber.
On inspection in October 1998 the monument was as described above. These tombs form part of a concentration of prehistoric monuments in the immediate vicinity, some of which were investigated by Grant (1995, 31-3). The closest of monuments in this complex include: a stone row (CL009-084006-), which lies c. 20m to the NW; and a standing stone (CL009-084032-), which lies c. 19m to the NNE.

CL009-098----:
On undulating ground in pasture, within a large multiperiod field system (CL009-059001-). Labelled as ‘Cromlech’ on the 1897 OS 25-inch plan and 1920 ed. of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 41) as a rubble-filled wedge tomb (L c. 3m; Wth at W 2-2.5m, narrowing to 1.7m at E; max. H at W 1.3m, sloping to min. 0.65m at E) embedded in a mound, of which only vestiges (c. 4m N-S; c. 1.25m E-W) survived at the E. The tomb was orientated E-W. Each of its sides consisted of a single limestone slab set on its long edge. The S sidestone (L 4.05m; H at W 1.25m, sloping to 0.85m at E; T 0.25m) leaned heavily to the S. Its top edge (L 3m) sloped evenly from W to E, with traces of dressing. The N sidestone (L 3.8m; H at W 1.3m, sloping to 0.65m at E; T 0.25-0.3m) also sloped from W to E, although the E part of its top edge was broken. The E endstone/backstone (L 1.6m; H 0.7m; T 0.15m) had a straight dressed top edge. De Valera and Ó Nualláin interpreted a flat-lying slab (L 1.4m; Wth 1.15m; T 0.2-0.25m) immediately to the W of the tomb as a fallen endstone, which would have partly closed the tomb entrance with a gap (c. 0.7m) between it and the N sidestone. CL009-112001-:
At the top of a small hillock in a depression, in hazel and briars. Named ‘Cromlech’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 34) as a well-preserved and fine wedge tomb embedded in the centre of a low suboval mound (13m E-W; 5-9m N–S; H c. 0.7m). The tomb was oriented E-W, and its chamber (int. dims. L 3.3m; Wth at W 2.1m, narrowing to 1.5m at E; H at W 1.55m, sloping to 1.05m at E) comprised single large sidestones at the N (L 3.65m; 1.4m H at W; 0.75m H at E; T 0.15-0.2m) and S (L 4.3m; 1.35m H at W, 0.55m H at E; T 0.3m), set upright on their long edges. Both slabs have straight, dressed top edges which slope evenly to the E. A transverse slab (L 1.45m; H 1.05m; T 0.1-0.15m) was set 0.6m from the E end of the sidestones; the E side of its straight top edge was also dressed (L 0.85m). There were two possibly intentional apertures along the edges of this slab, with chipping on the E face of their edges (see also Leask and Price 1935-37, 83). One possible opening at the S top corner was broken resulting in a jagged sloping edge (L 0.6m). The N edge of the slab had a curving indent (H 0.6m; max. Wth 0.2m) with a smooth, worn edge near the bottom and possible flaking near the top on its W face; the rest of the edge was jagged. The capstone (original L c. 4.3m) was broken. Its larger portion (L 3.3m; Wth 2.7m at W; Wth 1.7m at E; T 0.2m) still rested on the sidestones and transverse slab, while a smaller fragment (L 1.65m E-W; Wth 1.75m N-S; T 0.15-0.2m) lay fallen to the W, leaning against the N sidestone. At the W end of the sidestones were several disturbed, prostrate slabs: one (L 1.1m; Wth 0.65m) on the S and three (av. L 0.65m) on the N. These may have been remains of an entrance lining for the tomb chamber.
There appeared to be vestiges of an outer wall around the chamber at N, E and S, comprising slabs set parallel to the chamber sides. On the S was a slab (L 1.1m; H 0.35m; T 0.12m) standing 0.55m from the chamber, with two disturbed stones (L 0.55-1.05m; H 0.5m; T 0.1m) to its E. The N arc of the possible outer wall was represented by a N-leaning slab (L 1.4m; H 0.6m; T 0.1m), 0.65m from the chamber, with three possibly disturbed smaller stones (av. L 0.55m; H 0.55-0.9m) to its W. Finally, set 2m to the E of the chamber was a large slab (L 1.5m; H 1m; T 0.1m) oriented N-S and leaning to the W, with two loose stones (L 0.5m) resting against its W face.
Physically linking the E end of the main chamber and the N edge of the E outer wall-slab was a line of three small upright stones. The westernmost of these stones (L 0.35m; H 0.75m; T 0.1m) was set under the capstone; the other two (L 0.5-0.6m; H 0.2-0.4m; T 0.1m) were loose and perhaps not original. De Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) noted that this line of stones may have been the remnants of a second chamber, abutting the E end of the main chamber although they also noted that the evidence was scant and ambiguous; Westropp (1898, 256; 1906-07, 461) also offered this interpretation.
An inspection of the tomb in 1997 found it to be unaltered in the interim, apart from further overgrowth of hazel and briars, especially on the E side. …

CL010-006----:
On a level crag terrace in rough pasture, with land sloping to the W and rising to the NE and SE. Within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL005-160001-). Indicated and labelled ‘Ancient Grave’ on the Cassini edition (1920) of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 35-6) as a well-preserved and unusually small wedge tomb (L 1.6m; Wth at W 1.2m, narrowing to 0.75m at E; H at W 0.95m, sloping to 0.85m at E) that was embedded in the centre of a very poorly defined and partly grass-covered, circular cairn (diam. 7.5m; max. H c. 0.5m) of loose slabs (av. L 0.2-0.5m; max. L 1.5m). The tomb was orientated E–W and the footings of a later stone wall extended N from the NW corner. The tomb’s S sidestone (L 1.9m; H at W 1m, sloping to 0.9m at E; T 0.15m) was set in a gryke, and had straight edges. The N sidestone (L 1.95m; H 0.9m at W, sloping to 0.85m at E; T 0.15-0.2m) showed evidence of dressing on its top edge. There was a small packing stone (H 0.4m; L 0.3m) immediately to the N of this sidestone’s W end. A rectangular slab (L 1.2m; H 0.9m; T 0.1m) closed the W end of the tomb, standing at the same height as the sidestones which it almost touched. A small break (L 0.1m; H 0.1m) in the closing stone’s top N corner appeared to be accidental. The tomb’s capstone was broken, with a large fragment (L 1.3m; max. Wth at W 1.65m; T 0.1-0.2m) still apparently in original position at the W end of the tomb, resting on the sidestones and W closing stone. Two other probable capstone fragments lay at the E end of the tomb: a larger slab (L 1.6m) leaning against the N sidestone, and partly overlying another slab (L 1.35m) which leaned on the E end of the S sidestone’s top edge. There was another slab (L 1m; Wth 0.5m) within the tomb, the floor of which was strewn with small stones and was slightly lower than the ground level outside the tomb cairn. An inspection of the tomb in 1999 found it unaltered in the interim.

CL010-028----:
In an upland area of uneven semi-karst land in rough pasture, commanding wide views especially from SW to NE, within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL010-064001-). Named ‘Cromlech’ on the 1842 OS 6-inch map and the 1897 OS 25-inch plan. Drawn as a dolmen-like figure on the 1920 ed. of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 37) as a well-preserved wedge tomb (L 3.1m; Wth at W 2.05m, narrowing to 1.5m at E; H at W 1.35m, narrowing to 1.2m at E) orientated E-W, and embedded in the centre of a low oval-shaped mound (12.5m E-W; 8.5m N-S; max. H c. 0.6m) which was disturbed at the NW and SE by grass-covered field walls extending NW-SE. One slab (L 0.75m; H 0.1m) set on edge within the mound near its E side was proposed as a possible kerbstone (ibid.). The chamber sides each consisted of single slabs which were also set on their long edges. The S sidestone (L 3.5m; H at W 1.4m, sloping to 1.35m at E; T 0.2m) and the N sidestone (L at base 3.05m; L at top 3.55m; H 1.3m at W, sloping to 1.1m at E; T 0.2m) were dressed along their top edges, although the E end of the S sidestone was broken at the top. Westropp (1905, 223) recorded the N sidestone extending further to the E. The top edge of the W endstone (L 2.15m; H 1.35m; T 0.15m) was dressed straight; its N edge was also straight and its S edge was chipped, but it was unclear whether these profiles were intentional and ancient. There was a gap (0.35-0.6m) between this endstone and the S sidestone. The capstone was broken into two fragments (W piece L 2m; Wth 2.75m; T 0.2m; E piece L 3m; Wth 2.65m; T 0.2m) both resting on the sidestones with the E capstone fragment overlapping (L 0.2m) the W piece.
Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 37) proposed a double row of outer-walling around part of the tomb chamber. On the N side the straight inner line of this outer-walling consisted of three upright slabs (L 0.45-0.95; H 0.05-0.7m; T 0.1-0.15m) which converged with the chamber toward the E, while the more curving outer line comprised six slabs (L 0.3-0.8; av. H 0.25m; av. T 0.1m). Westropp (1905, 223) drew these rows continuing around the W side of the tomb. On the S side the outer-walling consisted of three stones (L 0.3-0.75m; H 0.1-0.35m; T 0.05-0.1m) which also converged with the E end of the tomb. To the E of the chamber were two less clearly defined lines of upright slabs (L 0.45-1.2m; av. H 0.25m; T 0.1m). Another slab (L 1.8m; H 1m; T 0.1m) set upright on its long edge and running W from the NW corner of the chamber was suggested as possibly part of the lining of the entrance (‘portico’) (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 37). The black earth floor of the chamber was strewn with stones, its W end being partly blocked by them. Westropp (1905, 223) drew a flat-lying ‘basin-stone’ (est. L c. 0.75m; Wth 0.6m) with five cupmarks on its upper surface, located in the SW corner of the tomb. He also (ibid.) described this wedge tomb as ‘recently inhabited’. An inspection of the tomb in 1999 found it unaltered in the interim.

CL010-064013-:
On a very slight rise in high (between 600’ and 653’) undulating rough pasture, within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL010-064001-), with fair views E-S-W-NE. Indicated as a rectangular feature and named ‘Dermot & Grania’s Bed’ on both the first edition (1842) and Cassini edition (1920) of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 46) as a very disturbed wedge tomb (est. min. L 3.1m E-W; Wth 1.2m at E) embedded in the centre of a low, roughly circular mound (12.5m N-S; 11.5m E-W; H 0.75-1.25m). The tomb appeared to have originally been orientated E-W. The N and E sides were still in situ, with possible remains of outer-walling at the NE and with a broken capstone lying beyond this to the NE. The N sidestone (L 3.3m; H 1.1m; T 0.15m) leaned inward (i.e., to the S), and was cracked near the W. Westropp (1905, 221) observed signs of hammer-dressing at the E. The E end of the tomb comprised three parallel slabs (L 1.15-1.7m; H 1-1.2m; T 0.1-0.15m). Just to the NE of these was an earthfast slab (L 1.4m; H 0.9m; T 0.1m) orientated NW-SE. Together with a second slab (L 0.7m; H 0.25m; T 0.1m) 0.5m to the E, a third slab (L 1.25m; H 1m; T 0.15m) just N of the N sidestone’s E end and a fourth slab (L 1.7m; H 1m; T 0.15m) leaning against the N side of the N sidestone, all were thought to possibly represent an outer-walling enclosing the tomb’s E end. Immediately to the NE lay two capstone fragments (W fragment L 2.3m; Wth 2.3m; T 0.2-0.3m; E fragment L 2.15m; Wth 1.7m; T 0.2-0.3m). Two smaller slabs lay near the capstone pieces, one (L 1.15m; T 0.1m) to the SE and the other (L 1.55m; Wth 0.95m; T 0.1m) to the NE. Westropp (ibid.) also found the capstone resting on the tomb’s side. An inspection in 1999 found the tomb to have remained as described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (op. cit.) . A cashel (CL010-064014-) lies c. 30m to the E.

CL010-064023-:
This wedge tomb is a National Monument (no. 270) in state care. On a SE-sloping, grass-covered crag in rough pasture, commanding wide views out NE-W and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL010-064001-). Marked as a rectangle and labelled ‘Dermot & Grania’s Bed’ on both the first (1842) and later, Cassini editions of the OS 6-inch map. Perhaps considerably damaged by fire c. 1880 about which Westropp (1896, 365; 1913, 247, Footnote 4) records, ‘… a long cromlech, much injured by fire [and] partially destroyed …’. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 47) as a partly damaged wedge tomb (L min. 2.7m; Wth at W 1.6m, narrowing to 1.3m at E) orientated ENE-WSW, and embedded in the semicircular remains of a low mound (c. 9m NW-SE; c. 4.5m NE-SW; max. H c. 0.5m) which was visible around the W end of the tomb. A modern drystone wall running NNW-SSE covered the E end of the tomb. This wall was part of a collapsed hut, collapse from which also appeared to have formed a grass-covered heap of stones just to the N of the tomb. This hut may relate to a reference to this tomb in the OS Letters of 1839, ‘under which many poor families have lived!’ (Comber 1997, 22).
The N and S sides of the tomb each comprised a single, large limestone slab set on its long edge. The very fine N slab (L 4.5m; H 1.37m at W, sloping to 1m at E; T 0.15-0.25m) was cracked 1.65m from its W end, and the top edge was worked on both sides. The S sidestone (L 3.25m; H 0.9m; T 0.1-0.15m) was broken with most of its top missing and its E end covered by the drystone wall collapse from a later hut. The W end of the tomb was closed by two slabs, one (L 1.05m; H 1m; T 0.1-0.15m) at the S set perpendicularly to the sidestones and with a broken top edge, and another (L 0.75m; H 1.2m; T 0.15-0.2m) at the N standing at a more oblique angle. The E end of the tomb was concealed by a later drystone wall. Many loose and broken slabs of diverse sizes (largest fragment L 1.75m; T 0.15m) were observed leaning at angles within the tomb chamber. Some of these were thought to possibly be pieces of the tomb’s capstone. Others appeared to be rubble from the later drystone hut abutting the E end of the tomb. An inspection of the tomb in 1999 found it unaltered in the interim.

CL010-092----:
On a gentle NW-facing slope in semi-karst rough pastureland and within an extensive field system (CL010-064001-). Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 48) as a very poorly preserved, SW-NE orientated wedge tomb (est. L min. 2.95m; Wth at W c. 1.2m, narrowing to est. 0.95m) embedded in a mound of which semicircular traces (c. 4m N-S; c. 2.7m E-W) were still present around the W side. The surviving fragments of the tomb chamber included the S sidestone which was still in its original position, as well as two flat-lying slabs. The S sidestone (L 2.95m; H 1.15m at W, sloping to 0.9m at E; T 0.25m) leaned heavily to the N, but retained its straight top edge which was dressed along the inside. To the S of its W end was a small, similarly E-W orientated stone (L 0.65m; T 0.1m) set on edge but embedded in the ground so that its top was flush with the ground surface. De Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) suggested that this may be a packing-stone or part of an outer-walling. Two larger flat-lying slabs (one on the other) were found to the N of the sidestone. Like Westropp (1905, 216), de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 48) concluded that the upper slab (L 2.9m; Wth 1.9m; T 0.25m) was the fallen capstone, while the prostrate slab under it (L 3.25m; Wth 1.4m at W, narrowing to 1.1m at E) was suggested to be the N sidestone, with its N side having been the slab’s top edge when erect. The position of this fallen N sidestone suggested to de Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) that the tomb was broader at the W. An inspection of the tomb in 1998 found it unaltered in the interim, although the small packing-stone/ outer wall stone was not noted. There are a large number of wedge tombs and other prehistoric remains in the vicinity (see Jones 2008), with several wedge tombs very close by: one (CL017-015005-) c. 73m to the S; another (CL017-015004-) c. 130m to the SW; and another (CL017-015006-) c. 154m to the WSW. There is also a megalithic structure (CL017-015001-) c. 122m to the S, and a cairn (CL017-015003-) c. 170m to the SSW.

CL010-093----:
On the E-facing slope of a low ridge of exposed karst and rough pasture. Not recorded on OS mapping. Indicated on Robinson’s map of the Burren (1977). Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 48) as a very poorly preserved wedge tomb almost entirely surrounded by an irregular mound (7.5m NE-SW; 5m NW-SE; max. H 1.25m), itself enclosed within an area (L 10m; Wth 8m) defined by the traces of a low bank – possibly the remains of a wall. The only upstanding element of the tomb chamber was its large, S sidestone (L 3m; H 1m; T 0.1m), orientated SW-NE. The SW part (L 1.75m) of the slab’s top edge was broken while the remaining E portion appeared to be dressed, and sloped from W to E. There was a natural hole in the upper centre of the sidestone (also noted by Westropp; 1905, 217). CL010-110----:
Within a thicket of trees and bushes on an improved pasture shelf overlooking lower ground c. 45m to the SE which is liable to flood from Coolreash Lough to the N. Indicated and labelled ‘Cromlech’ on the both the first (1842) and later, Cassini edition (1920) of the OS 6-inch map. Westropp (1905, 212) noted that this wedge tomb was still inhabited into then-recent times, ‘forming the bedroom of a small cabin’. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 49) as a well-preserved but overgrown trapezoidal wedge tomb (L 2.4m; Wth 1.45m at SW, narrowing to 1.2m at NE; H 1.6m at SW, sloping to 1.2m at NE) embedded in the centre of an oval mound (c. 11m NE-SW; 8m NW-SE; max. H c. 1m) on which lay many stones, perhaps including some from field clearance. Trees and bushes grew on and around the mound, and its SE part was obscured by a later small stone enclosure. The tomb chamber was orientated NE-SW, with a single slab on each side. Both sidestones leaned slightly inward and bore traces of dressing on their top edges, which sloped from SW to NE and were longer at their protruding top edges than at their base (NW sidestone L 3.05m at top, 2.3m at base; max. H c. 1.4m; T 0.1-0.2m; SE sidestone surviving L 1.45m at base; max. H c. 1.16m; T 0.15-0.2m), although the SW end of the SE sidestone appeared to have been broken relatively recently. Westropp (op. cit.) observed that the inner faces of these sidestones had been ‘picked to a smooth surface which I hardly ever noted elsewhere, even to a much lesser degree.’ The fine rectangular NE backstone (H 1.15m; L 1.1m; T 0.15m) also leaned inward slightly, and seemingly had dressed top and side edges. There was a gap (0.12m) between the backstone and the lower parts of each sidestone (0.12m from NW sidestone; 0.3m from SE sidestone). A large displaced slab (H 1.85m; Wth 0.75m; T 0.1-0.2m) leaned against the SW end of the NW sidestone, partly closing the SW end of the chamber. The roofstone (L 3.25m; Wth 2m at SW, narrowing to 1.4m at NE; T 0.15m) completely covered the chamber, resting on the sidestones and the NE backstone. Westropp (op. cit.) described ‘curious “footmarks” and other depressions’ on this roofstone. A later wall extended SW from the SW corner of the tomb chamber. Inspections in 1999 and 2007 found the tomb to be unaltered in the interim, apart from a thickening of overgrowth. In 2007, a path to the tomb from the SE was created.

In rough pasture on a gentle W-facing slope near the base of Roughan hill. It is recorded in the Megalithic Survey as CL141 (Ó Nualláin 1989, 134) and by Jones et. al. (1996, 100) as site B.
A poorly preserved wedge tomb with a SSW-aligned chamber (min. L 4.6m; Wth c. 1.9m at the W end) surrounded by a low cairn (diam. c. 9m; max. H 0.6m). The enclosure is Jones’ (2011, 39) Farm RH5 which, along with at least two other enclosures on Roughan Hill, has been shown through excavation to be of Beaker and Early Bronze Age date, a date consistent with the wedge tombs.

CL016-061002-:
On the N-facing slope of a low ridge with rising karst to the S and E, at the SE end of the central Burren plateau and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL017-180----). This is the most northerly wedge tomb in a group of four wedge tombs (see also CL016-061001-, CL016-061004- and CL016-061003-) and a quarry (CL016-061005-) and was excavated in 2016 as part of a larger project to explore prehistoric society in the west of Ireland (Ó Maoldúin 2017, 6). The wedge tombs are collectively identified as ‘cromlechs’ on the 1840 and 1916 OS 6-inch maps. The group of wedge tombs is described by O’Donovan in 1839 as ‘three cromleachs in the same field, one of which is prostrate’ (Comber 1997, 20). Referred to by Westropp (1898, 357) as the ‘N.E cromlech’ which must once have been a ‘fine example’ with the remaining portion of the roofstone described as a ‘plank’ leaning against the S side of the chamber. Westropp (1898, 357) also describes the fallen N side as having  ‘strangely regular natural channels across it’. The structure is included in the ‘Reabachan Group of Dolmens’ (Westropp 1905, 213) and is described as ‘defaced’ with measurements given for the remaining S end of the chamber (L 4.6m; H 1.7m at W; H 2.7m at E; T 0.27m) (Westropp 1907, 464). This site is recorded in the Megalithic Survey as CL. 59 (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 49-50) and the following details are drawn from there.
A poorly preserved wedge tomb with a SW orientation and with one sidestone remaining at the S end of a ruined chamber (L 4.7m; Wth 1.4m at back; Wth 2m at front; H 1.1m at back; H 1.95m at front). The S sidestone (max. L 4.7m; H 0.5-1.7m; T c.  0.3m) was broken into three parts (2.5m; 1.7m; 0.5m) with evidence for cobble percussion along its upper edge. It was estimated to be over 4 tonnes in weight and distinguishes this site as one of the largest wedge tombs on Roughan hill (Ó Maoldúin 2017, 27). The eroded surface of this stone faced the interior of the chamber and the natural channels identified by Westropp (1898, 357) have been identified as runnels. The sidestone slopes from W to E and is noticeably steeper than the other wedge tombs identified on Roughan hill. The site was found to have been disturbed by badgers during the 2016 excavation, but a substantial amount of cremated and unburnt bone was recovered from the chamber area.
Two stones are located outside the S sidestone to the E. The most easterly of these (L 0.75m; H 0.1m; T 0.15m) is set in place and may be a packing-stone but the most westerly stone (L 0.8m; H 0.45m; T 0.05-0.25m) is loose. Two further displaced stones with similar dimensions (L 1.25m; T 0.2m) lean against the inner face of the S sidestone at the E end and a slab (L 1.45m; H 1.8m; T 0.2m) which also leans against the inner face of the S sidestone at the W end may be all that remains of the roofstone. To the north of this stone, an almost prostrate slab (L 1.7m; Wth 1.3m; T 0.15-0.25m) overlaps a similar slab (L 1.1m; Wth 1.1m; T 0.2-0.3m) and both have straight smooth edges at the S and may be the remains of the N end of the chamber. …
CL016-061003-:
On a NW-facing slope in a flat field at the SE end of the central Burren plateau and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL017-180----). This is the most southerly wedge tomb in a group of four wedge tombs (see also CL016-061001-, CL016-061002- and CL016-061004-) and a quarry (CL016-061005-). The wedge tombs are collectively identified as ‘cromlechs’ on the 1840 and 1916 OS 6-inch maps. Described by O’Donovan in 1839 as one of ‘three cromleachs in the same field, one of which is prostrate’ (Comber 1997, 20). Described by Westropp (1898, 357) as ‘a small cist’ (3.6m; 2.4m) ‘nearly embedded in a mound, and surrounded by seven slabs’ (H 0.91m). The measurements for the monument were later rectified by Westropp (1905, 214) who clarified that ‘the dimensions refer to its mound and circle of slabs - ‘This cist, in fact, is of three slabs, each only a little over 5 feet long; the east slab has either been removed or its place was taken by a block in the outer ring near the end of the side slabs’. The site is included in the ‘Reabachan Group of Dolmens’ (Westropp 1907, 464). This site is recorded in the Megalithic Survey as CL. 62 (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 51-2) and the following details are drawn from there.
A wedge tomb with a poorly preserved WSW-ENE aligned, partially collapsed chamber (est. L c. 2m) in the centre of a mound (10m E-W; 9m N-S). The N sidestone (L 2m; H 0.9m at W end; H 0.7m at E; T 0.15m) of the chamber is dressed along the top edge and the S sidestone of the chamber has collapsed inwards (L 1.95m) and lies under the displaced roofstone. A closing stone at the W (L 1.8m; H 1m; T c. 0.1-0.15m) remains in position but leans outwards and extends beyond the N sidestone. A slab at the E end of the chamber (L 0.75m; H 0.55m; T 0.1m) may be a backstone but may also be part of the outer-walling which surrounds the chamber. The roofstone (L 2.1m; Wth 1.75m at W; Wth 1.3m at E; T 0.15-0.2m) rests on the N sidestone and slopes to the S where it disappears into the mound. The outer-walling which surrounds the chamber is best preserved at the S where three stones remain in position and comprise a stone at E (L 0.8m; H 0.7m; T 0.15m), a middle stone (L 0.85m; H 0.5m; T 0.1m) and a stone at W (L 0.6m; H 0.65m; T 0.15m), all of which lean outwards. A curved line of stones surrounds the W end of the chamber and comprises a S stone (L 0.6m; H 0.8m; T 0.1m), a middle stone (L 1.15m; est. H 0.7m) which is almost prostrate and a third stone (L 0.95m; H 0.9m; T 0.15m). There are two stones to the N of the chamber, the most westerly of which (L 0.55m; H 0.3m; T 0.1m) is loose  and the most easterly of which (L 1.05m; T 0.1m; est. H 0.9m) leans outwards and may be displaced (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 51-2).
This wedge tombs is part of the Roughan hill group which fall within the four townlands of Parknabinnia, Leana, Caherfadda and Commons North and have been acknowledged as the densest concentration of wedge tombs in Ireland (Jones et al. 2015, 5). …
CL016-061004-:
On a NW-facing slope in a flat field at the SE of the central Burren plateau and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL017-180----). Within a group of four wedge tombs (see also CL016-061001-, CL016-061002- and CL016-061003-) and a quarry (CL016-061005-). The wedge tombs are collectively identified as ‘cromlechs’ on the 1840 and 1916 OS 6-inch maps. Described by O’Donovan in 1839 as one of ‘three cromleachs in the same field, one of which is prostrate’ (Comber 1997, 20). Described by Westropp (1898, 357) as ‘a fine cromlech’ which tapers eastwards in height  (L 5.2m; max. H 1.95; H 1.7m) ‘with a curious angular gap in the west slab’. The measurement for the length of the monument was later rectified (L 4.2m) by Westropp (1905, 213-14) and it is included in the ‘Reabachan Group of Dolmens’ and described as ‘perfect’ (Westropp 1907, 464). This site is recorded in the Megalithic Survey as CL. 61 (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 51) and the following details are drawn from there.
A well-preserved wedge tomb with a WSW-ENE aligned chamber (L 2.95m; Wth 2m at W end; H 1.2m at W end; Wth 1.7m at E end; H 0.85m at E end) which decreases in height and width from W to E and is surrounded by a mound (9.5m E-W; 7m N-S). The N and S sides of the chamber comprise single slabs. The N sidestone leans inwards (L 4.5m; H 1.1m at W end; H 0.85m at E end; T 0.1-0.2m) and the top edge of this stone (L 3.6m) bears the marks of flaking and has been broken away in the E corner. The S sidestone (L 4.2m; H 1.2m at W; H 0.9m at E; T 0.15m) also appears to have been flaked along the top edge (L 3.4m) but it is unclear in both of these instances if this flaking is representative of intentional dressing. The closing stone (L 1.4m; H 1.05m; T 0.15m) at the W end of the chamber is level with the S sidestone but there is a gap (L 0.45m) between it and the N sidestone. This closing stone is also flaked along the top. The E end of the chamber is closed by a single slab (L 1.15m; H 0.95m; T 0.15-0.2m) which is the same height as both the N and S sidestones. The top edge of the E stone at N has been broken away and there is a gap (L 0.4m) between the N edge of the E stone and the N sidestone.
In the W end of the chamber, both the N and S sidestones support the portion of the roofstone (L 1.6m; Wth 2.85m at W end; Wth 3m at E end; T 0.2-0.3m) which remains. The weight of the roofstone rests on a stone (max. dims. 0.15m; T 0.5m) which sits on the top of the N sidestone and the roofstone also partially rests on the W end of the chamber. The E end of the roofstone is broken and stone fragments (max. dims. 0.75m) within the chamber may be portions of it (De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 51).
This wedge tomb is part of the Roughan hill group which falls within the four townlands of Parknabinnia, Leana, Caherfadda and Commons North and have been acknowledged as the densest concentration of wedge tombs in Ireland (Jones et al. 2015, 5). …
CL016-093----:
On the N-facing S slopes of the shallow basin of the River Fergus c. 35m to the W of a cashel (CL016-094----). Views are limited except to the NE where the E Burren hills are visible. Indicated on the 1840 OS 6-inch map and named ‘Dermot & Grania’s Bed’ on the 1916 ed. Referred to by Westropp (1905, 210-11) as ‘Labba’ or ‘Lobba yermuth’ and described as tapered and sloping to the E (L 4.5-4.8m) with an ESE-WNW axis. He described the S sidestone (L 3.07m; Wth 1.3m; T 0.18-0.24m) as having a hole in its side and the W extent is identified as an entrance. Westropp later (1906, 465) describes the site as ‘collapsed’. Recorded in the Megalithic Survey as CL.64 (De Valera and Ó’Nualláin 1961, 53) with the following details.
A wedge tomb with a WNW-ESE aligned chamber (L c. 3.5m; Wth c. 2m) which has been cut by the base of a stone fence at SE. The N side of the chamber comprises  a single slab (max. L c. 5m; max. H c. 1.5m; T 0.2-0.25m) which has collapsed outwards and broken into two pieces. The S side of the chamber comprises a single slab that has broken into two pieces. The W portion of the S sidestone (L 3.15m; H 1.35m at W; H 1.15 at E; T 0.15m) leans outwards and is chipped along its top edge (L 2.8m). The E portion of the S sidestone (L 2.1m; max. H 0.9m; T 0.15m) is out of line with the W portion and a stone set outside and to the W (L 0.9m; H 0.3m; T 0.2m) may be a packing-stone or an outer wall stone. The W extent of the chamber comprises a single slab (L 1.5m; H 1.35m; T 0.15-0.2m) which leans outwards. The top end of this stone is level with the height of the W portion of the S sidestone. A broken slab in the chamber may be a portion of the roofstone. The backstone in the E (L 1.3m; T 0.1-0.15m; max. H c. 1m) leans to the S and a broken slab (L 2.05m; Wth c. 0.75m; T 0.15m) which leans against it may be another portion of the roof-slab. Two stones located 1.7m to the E of the backstone may be all that remain of an outer wall. Both the N stone (L 0.5m; H 0.2m; T 0.1m) and the S stone (L 0.95m; H 0.4m; T 0.2m) lean heavily towards the E.

CL016-130----:
On a gentle NW-facing slope of Roughan Hill and within an extensive multiperiod field system (CL017-180----). It is recorded by Jones and Walsh (1996, 88) as Site A and the following details are taken from there.
A damaged wedge tomb with a ruined WNW-ESE-aligned chamber (L 2.5m; Wth 1.5m at E) comprising a single side stone on the N side and the E portion of a sidestone at the S. The top of the N sidestone slopes to the E and there are three packing-stones at its base on the N side. The S sidestone has collapsed into the chamber area and lies beneath the broken roofstone. A large slab in the W end of the chamber may be an endstone and multiple displaced and broken slabs in the vicinity may be the remains of the roofstone and broken S sidestone. Traces of a mound are visible along the S side of the monument.
This tomb is part of the Roughan hill group, in Parknabinnia, Leana, Caherfadda and Commons North townlands, acknowledged as the densest concentration of wedge tombs in Ireland (Jones et al. 2015). Excavations have been carried out at three wedge tombs in the area: CL017-180002- (Ó Maoldúin 2015), CL017-009---- (Ó Maoldúin 2017) and CL016-061002- (Ó Maoldúin 2022) and have confirmed their date of construction as Chalcolithic to Early Bronze Age (Ó Maoldúin pers. comm.).

CL016-170----:
The monument stands on south-facing gently-sloping ground near the southern end of Parknabinna ridge overlooking the valley of the River Fergus. The land comprises extensive areas of outcropping rock and the field in which the tomb stands was reclaimed between 2005 and 2010. The portal tomb (CL016-048----) in the same townland stands c. 250m to the NW. The monument is ruined and the surviving remains consist of a two-chambered gallery (L 2.6m) opening to the E. Entry to the E chamber (L 1.8m) is marked by a single, tall transversely-set jamb-stone (1.8m H). Immediately W of this a large roofstone (2.25m by 1.9m) covers the chamber and rests at an angle against the segmenting jamb-stone and N sidestone. This stone is set at an angle to the line of the gallery and overlaps the corresponding N sidestone of the second chamber to the W leaving a gap of only 0.4m between the jamb and sidestone. The W chamber (L. 1.4m; Wth 1.7m) is represented by a single surviving sidestone on the N and S and is closed by a backstone at the W. An expanse of outcropping rock rises immediately W of the backstone and this would have inhibited any extension of the gallery in this direction. The possibility that the gallery extended further to the E cannot be excluded but, given the tall jamb-stone at this end, does not seem likely. There is no evidence of any structural stones to the N of the jamb and the monument appears to have had various drystone walling insertions and accretions which hinder a full interpretation of the structure. The tomb appears to be set in a low stony mound but it is difficult to define any edge with certainty due to the fact that the field has been reclaimed and clearance piled up around it, especially at the W end of the extant remains where a large section of reclaimed rock has been set upright. The two-chamber design and transversely-set jambs have obvious affinities with many of those in the court tomb galleries. That said, the monument lacks any evidence of a court and the large roofstone is more usually associated with portal tombs: the monument clearly displays influences from both architectural traditions. Interpretation as a possible court tomb is suggested but this is purely tentative and a proper elucidation of the monument must await further investigation.

CL017-008002-:
In rough pasture on a plateau which slopes gently down to the W and N and offering wide views out S-E. Indicated and labelled ‘Cromlech’ on the Cassini edition (1920) of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 54-5) as a well-preserved wedge tomb (int. dims. c. 1.8m NE-SW; Wth 0.75m) orientated NE-SW and embedded in the centre of an oval-shaped mound (c. 7.3m E-W; 5m N-S; est. H c. 0.5m). The N sidestone (L 2.3m; H 0.75m at SW, sloping to 0.65m at NE; T 0.15m) was cracked 1.5m from its SW end. The parallel S sidestone opposite (L 1.85m; H 0.7; T 0.2m) was also noted as sloping regularly down from SW to NE. The backstone (L 0.7m; H 0.6m; T 0.07m) at the NE end had a vertical crack through its centre; the top edge also appeared broken, such that the slab stood to 0.3m below the level of the sidestones (ibid.). The displaced capstone (L 1.85m; Wth 1.6m; T 0.15m) lay immediately to the NE of the tomb. Another prostrate slab (L 1.3m; T 0.15m) just to the E may have been part of the capstone. The interior of the tomb chamber was paved with slabs (L 0.5m) which appeared to have been laid in relatively recent times (ibid.). An inspection of the tomb in 1998 found it unaltered in the interim, except that there appeared to be elements of a kerb visible on the S side of the mound, 2.7m from the S sidestone where two stones (one L 0.8m; H 0.5m; Wth 0.2m) ran parallel with the side of the tomb. Another stone running N-S to the W of the tomb is less certain as a kerbstone.

CL017-009----:
On a gentle SW-facing slope in rough pasture and exposed limestone pavement near the top of Roughan Hill, offering wide views from SE-SW-NW. Indicated as a circular feature and labelled ‘Carn’ on the first edition (1842) of the OS 6-inch map. Marked as a smaller cairn on the OS 25-inch plan (1897) and the Cassini edition (1920) of the OS 6-inch map, with the label ‘Cromlech & Carn’ on the latter. Westropp (1906-1907, 453) noted that the cairn covering the tomb chamber was removed some time after 1839. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 55) as a very well-preserved wedge tomb (int. dims. L 2.3m SW-NE; Wth 1.6m at SW, 1.3m at NE; av. H 1.25m) in the centre of a grass-covered circular mound (av. diam. 16m; est. H c. 0.5m), the stones of which were visible to the N and W of the tomb, and they considered a pile of stones and earth still on top of the in situ capstone to be a remnant of the cairn. The NE-SW orientated wedge tomb comprises a NW sidestone (L 4.3m; H 1.2m at SW, 0.9m at NE; T 0.2-0.25m) and SE sidestone (L 3.55m; H 1.3m at SW, 1.1m at NE; T 0.15-0.25m), both dressed on their top edges which slope evenly from SW to NE. The NE backstone (L 1.2m; H 1.2m; T 0.15m) has worked side and top edges, and fits closely against the sidestones and capstone. Two slabs mostly block the SW end of the tomb. One of these blocking stones (L 1.35m; H 1.35m; T 0.1m) at the W neatly abuts the NW sidestone and has a straight dressed edge on this side and at its top, which reaches roof level (ibid.). This blocking stone extends more than halfway across the chamber entrance. Overlapping this slab for 0.5m at its base is the W blocking stone (L 0.85m; H 1m; T 0.1-0.2m) which extends across the chamber entrance from the SE sidestone and leans outwards. The large, irregular-shaped capstone (L 3.15m; Wth 2.7m at SW, 1.8m at NE; T 0.15-0.25m) rests on the backstone, the NW sidestone and the W blocking stone, and slopes from SW to NE (ibid.). Its SE edge is almost flush with the outer face of the sidestone below, while its NW side overhangs up to 0.75m beyond the NW sidestone. De Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) found the chamber floor covered with small stone debris.
In 2017, the interior of the chamber and part of the surrounding cairn were excavated (Ó Maoldúin 2022). The chamber was found to contain the semi-articulated skeletal remains of at least one adult, additional fragments of disturbed unburnt and burnt human bone, animal bone, firespots, clay pipe fragments, a post-medieval iron splitting wedge and modern detritus. Removal of sod surrounding the tomb revealed traces of the circular stone cairn (diam. c. 13m) the best preserved portion (W of the tomb) comprising stones ‘laid in a radial pattern or widening concentric circles’, many of which were laid on edge leaning toward the tomb chamber (ibid.). Several large kerbstones (max. L 1.4m) were laid flat around the cairn’s edge. The cairn was not fully excavated but in areas of previous disturbance, sections were excavated to bedrock. …
CL017-012----:
On a W-facing slope in mixed rough pasture and exposed limestone pavement. Drawn and labelled as ‘Cromlech’ on both the first (1842) and Cassini (1920) editions of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 54) as a well-preserved wedge tomb (L 3.5m; Wth 1.9m at front, narrowing to 1.3m at rear; av. H 1.5m) orientated SW-NE. The tomb chamber comprised a NW sidestone (L 4.5m; H 1.6m at SW, sloping to 1.1m at the NE; T 0.25m) with its top edge dressed (ibid.). The SE sidestone (L 3.6m; H 1.6m at SW, sloping to 1.35m at the NE; T 0.2-0.25m) was also dressed on its top edge. The close-fitting but slightly outward-leaning backstone (L 1.3m; H 1.45m; T 0.15m) at the NE end had a gap (Wth 0.45m; H 0.4m) in the lower SE corner which appeared to be a relatively recent break (ibid.). The tomb’s large capstone (L 3.75m; Wth 2.5m) was cracked through c. 1.5m from its SW end, as were the sidestones. There were remains of outer-walling at the SE of the tomb, where a line (L c. 4m) of three slabs set on edge ran N-S, almost parallel with the chamber’s SE sidestone at a distance of c. 1.1m away. The rectangular NE slab (L 1.35m; H 1.3m; T 0.15m) in this outer-walling was larger than the central (L 1.4m; H 0.55m) and SW (L 0.6m; H 0.1m; T 0.12m) stones. The chamber floor was uneven. According to Westropp (1905, 217), the tomb was inhabited during the mid-19th century ‘with a small side-annexe to the south, once adopted as a habitation for the family pig’, and mortar filled the gaps between its structural slabs (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 54). The tomb was also incorporated into several later stone walls, one of which obscured the NW face of the central slab in the tomb’s outer-walling (ibid.). An inspection of the tomb in 1998 found it unaltered in the interim, but it was observed that the surrounding later drystone walls are wide and double-faced. One runs N-S to the W of the chamber, then turns E just to the S of the chamber and almost blocks it off, and then turns S again.

CL017-015004-:
On a knoll on a W-facing slope (above the 500’ contour) in mixed rough pasture and exposed limestone pavement. Indicated and labelled ‘Cromlechs’ on both the first (1842) and Cassini (1920) of the OS 6-inch map. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 55-56) as a damaged wedge tomb (int. dims. L 2m; Wth 1.3m at SW, narrowing to 0.85m at NE; min. H 1.1m at SW, 0.65m at NE), orientated NE-SW and embedded in a subcircular mound (L 10m; Wth 8m; H c. 1m) which appeared to be composed of  small overlapping slabs. A later stone wall crossed the cairn, incorporating the NE end of the tomb chamber (ibid.). The chamber remains included both sidestones, the backstone, a blocking stone and a broken and displaced capstone. The SE sidestone’s (L 2.9m; T 0.12m) upper portion was broken off except at the E (H 0.85m), where the top edge was dressed on both sides (ibid.). Westropp (1905, 216; 1906-1907, 464) may have observed a hole in the W end of this sidestone. The NW sidestone (L 2.5m; max. H 0.9m; T 0.12m) was also broken at the W (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 55-56). Both sidestones sloped to the NE. Outside the SW end of the NW sidestone was a small earthfast pillar-like stone (L 0.3m; Wth 0.2m; H 0.35m). The backstone (L 1.4m; H 0.65m; T 0.1-0.15m) had a gap (Wth 0.35m; H 0.25m) in its top NE corner. This gap was dressed, as was the top edge of the slab. However, the relative positions of the SE sidestone and the backstone were such that this gap was outside the chamber and could not provide access to it (ibid.). The blocking stone (L 1.05m; H 1.1m; T 0.12m) at the SW end of the chamber was dressed on its NW edge and along part of the top edge. It fit closely against the NW sidestone but was 0.35m from the SE sidestone (ibid.). One large piece (L 1.2m; Wth 1.4m; T 0.1-0.15m) of the broken and displaced capstone leaned against the unbroken top edge of the NW sidestone, and was partly buried in the small stones within the chamber. Another probably displaced slab (L 1.5m; H 0.7m; T 0.12m) stood almost upright in the SW end of the chamber. De Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid., 56) suggested that there may have been remains of kerbing around the tomb: about 2m to the SE of the chamber side three slabs (L 0.55-1.45m; H 0.1-0.35m; T 0.05-0.1m) protruded from the mound, leaning to the N and co-aligned with the chamber (orientated NE-SW), while another slab (L 1.1m; H 0.45m; T 0.1m) was set c. 2m to the SW of the tomb, orientated NW-SE. An inspection of the tomb in 1998 found it unaltered in the interim. A megalithic structure (CL017-015001-) lies c. 78m to the ESE. There is a cairn (CL017-015003-) c. 79m to the SE, another wedge tomb (CL017-015005-) c. 85m to the ENE, another (CL017-015006-) c. 88m to the NW, and yet another (CL010-092----) c. 130m to the NE.
Compiled by: Gearóid Conroy and Conn Herriott
Date of upload: 23-10-2025
CL017-015006-:
On a gentle NW-facing slope in mixed rough pasture and hazel scrub. This small wedge tomb (L 1.6m; Wth c. 1m; H 0.8m) is embedded in the N sector of a low circular cairn (diam. 5.5m) retained by kerbstones, some of which (L 0.8-0.9m) at S have fallen outwards. Later stone walls radiate SW, SE and N from the tomb, with a barely perceptible D-shaped enclosure (int. dims. 4m E-W; 3m N-S) defined by a grass-covered wall abutting the N side of the SE wall and partly overlying the E side of the cairn. The NW quadrant of the cairn has been removed, in the area between the walls radiating N and SW from the tomb. The tomb chamber comprises two almost parallel slabs set on edge, orientated roughly E-W. The N sidestone (L 1m; H 0.8m; T 0.15-0.2m) is orientated WNW-ESE. The S sidestone (L 1.6m; H 0.7m) is positioned 0.65m away from the N sidestone at the W, and 0.5m away at the E. Within the cairn to the N of the chamber are two upright stones in a N-S line, which may be part of the later wall extending N from the tomb. To the S of the tomb and within the cairn is a small platform (c. 1.2m N-S; c. 0.55m E-W) defined by scarps on the W and S sides. To the S of this platform there are several upright stones at the centre of the cairn, which do not appear to be part of another tomb chamber. There is another wedge tomb (CL017-015004-) c. 88m to the SE.
Compiled by: Gearóid Conroy and Conn Herriott
Date of upload: 23-10-2025
CL017-046----:
On a very low, overgrown E-W ridge in pasture, with limestone pavement c. 140m to the N. Drawn and labelled as ‘Cromlech’ on both the first (1842) and Cassini (1920) editions of the OS 6-inch map. This megalithic tomb comprises a single, large upright slab, orientated N-S (L 2.5m N-S; H 1.2m; T 0.2m) set in a cairn (10.6m N-S; 8.2m E-W; H c. 0.6m). There are two large stones lying prone adjacent to the upright slab: one (L 2.4m; Wth 1.8m) immediately to the E, and the second (L 1.7m; Wth 1.1m) just to the SE. A third, smaller slab (L 1.3m; Wth 0.6m) lies further to the E, in the vicinity of which there is also a NW-SE orientated pavement-like cluster (L 2.3m; Wth 1.6m) of smaller flat-lying, flat-topped slabs (each c. L 0.3m; Wth 0.3m) which are unrelated to the tomb. Westropp (1905, 212) interpreted the upright stone as the W side of a ‘dolmen’. De Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 57) proposed that this may have been a wedge tomb, observing that the slab set on edge resembled the sidestones of many wedge tombs in NW Clare. There is a cist (CL017-076----) c. 260m to the W, and a wedge tomb (CL010-110----) c.685m to the ENE.
Compiled by: Gearóid Conroy and Conn Herriott
Date of upload: 13-10-2025
CL017-072----:
At the highest point on a hill, with wide panoramic views. Indicated and named ‘Coad Stone’ on the 1842 and 1920 eds. of the OS 6-inch map. This well-preserved limestone standing stone (H 2.25m; basal dims. L 0.4m; Wth 0.2m; upper dims. L 0.5m; Wth 0.2m) is oriented NW-SE. Its top is pointed at the SE and slopes down to the NW (H 1.75m). There are solution holes in the stone, which appears to be set on a vaguely defined low bank at the E side of a slight hollow (diam. c. 7m); the latter does not appear to be ancient. A field wall is built against the standing stone. The standing stone and wall lie on/near the E perimeter of a mid-19th century racecourse (CL017-202001-). Westropp (1906-1907, 470-1) suggested that this standing stone may have marked the E limit of the lands of medieval Coad church (CL017-066001-), c. 640m to the W. He also asserted that the townland name Coad (from Comfhod, ‘equal length’) usually means ‘tombstone’, and he recorded the local name “Clochliagaun” for this standing stone. He related (ibid.) an account that it was ‘overthrown by a Kilnaboy treasure-seeker’ in 1854, and was re-erected in 1894 by fellow antiquarian George MacNamara and his brother, who ‘found no traces of burial at its foot’.

CL017-180002-:
The remains of this monument were described as follows (Jones et al. 1996, Site E): 'The tomb is very ruined and consists of a damaged chamber, aligned east-north-east/west-south-west, incorporated in a sub-circular mound. The northern side of the chamber consists of two stones, a small low block at the west and beside it a long slab. The top of the slab slopes from west to east. An inclined slab set inside the line of the northern side crosses the west end of the chamber. Several displaced slabs are exposed along the south side of the chamber. The original dimensions of the chamber cannot be obtained but it was at least 2m long. The tomb is surrounded by a substantial mound between 0.6m and 1m high. Protruding from the mound at the west and south is a series of almost prostrate slabs which may be the remains of a kerb'.
Excavations in 2015 (licence no. 15E0053) by Ros Ó Maoldúin (Ó Maoldúin 2015) revealed that the chamber was centrally set within a circular kerbed cairn, c. 7m in diameter. A second inner kerb-line, most obvious to the rear of the chamber and c. 4m in diameter, was exposed within the cairn. A substantial amount of cremated and unburnt human bone was recovered, mostly from the chamber though no obvious grave goods were found there. An unburnt, and partially articulated, adult was uncovered within the stones stacked up outside the NNW end of the chamber. Several lithics, mostly debitage, were recovered from in and around the cairn but could not be linked stratigraphically to the chamber burials (Ó Malodúin 2015).
Compiled by: Paul Walsh
Date of upload: 15 September 2016

In rocky bogland on the E edge of a gravel quarry on the W edge of a ridge in mountain terrain with extensive views from W to N. Listed in the RMP (1996) as ‘Megalithic structure’. A sandstone conglomerate orientated SW-NE (H 1.45m rising to 1.8m at SW; Wth 0.85m; T 0.6-0.75m at base, tapering toward the top (0.15m)) situated dangerously close (0.4m) to a quarry edge and in close proximity and at right angles to a glacial erratic (2m to S). The adjacent erratic (L 2.8m; Wth 1.8m; H 1.8m) is also a sandstone conglomerate and is one of the largest boulders on the ridge. Although natural it is clearly associated with the standing stone.

CL027-018----:
In a small valley of poorly drained rough pasture, on a low, W-facing shelf directly overlooking a small stream to W, which is overlooked by low limestone cliffs to E and W. The monument is depicted and named on the OS 25-inch map and 1920 edition of the OS 6-inch map as ‘Dermot and Grania’s Bed’. The monument consists of the remains of a gallery (overall dims. c. 5.6m N-S; c. 2.2m E-W) which appears to survive as per the description provided in the Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland (De Valera & Ó Nualláin 1961, 74-5). Two large in situ orthostats define the E side and one large and three small orthostats form the W side of the tomb. Two sod-covered stones form the back stones at the N end, the easternmost of which is tilted forward to S. The largest orthostat (L 2.05m; T 0.34m; H 1.25m) is located at the N end of the W side. A substantial flagstone (L 2.2m; min. Wth 1.7m; min. T 0.18m) is lying partially sod-covered at the N end of the monument. This is likely to be a displaced capstone which has slipped off the top of the monument, probably when the stones on the E side moved out of position. A second partially sod-covered flagstone is located to the immediately W and may have been a secondary capstone. A number of large stones located on the downslope between the monument and the stream are obscured by vegetation and may once have formed part of the monument. The interior is quite sunken and uneven, possibly having been disturbed in antiquity. It is much obscured by vegetation including trees and may have animal activity in the form of burrows. A slight mound (H 0.25m) enclosed the gallery N-SSW. This monument in not of a typical E-W orientation and based on Westropp’s plan, it could be interpreted as a ‘court cairn’ (ibid). A wedge tomb (CL027-019001-) is located c. 450m to SE.

CL027-019001-:
On generally level ground, in a small haggard, in the angle between a walled garden (long-axis N-S) to E and an outbuilding (long-axis E-W) to S. Reasonable views to W and N, over slightly lower ground, yet limited to E and S due to upstanding structures. Depicted and named ‘Cromlech’ on all OS historic mapping. The monument appears to have been constructed on a pavement of limestone, which is situated c. 0.2m above the external ground level. A well-preserved wedge tomb (6m NE-SW; 4m NW-SE) open to SW. The monument is defined by three upright in-situ orthostats to NW and what appear to be three upright orthostats to SE, of which the two to the rear seem slightly displaced and largely obscured by dense briars. A large in-situ capstone covers the rear of the tomb. Its weight is borne on the rear sidestone to NW and SE. Across the centre and front of the tomb, a substantial displaced capstone has fallen inwards and is almost upright. Its weight appears to have been borne on the two central sidestones to NW and SE. Together the four central and rear sidestones taper to form the wedge shape of the tomb, as can be seen clearly in the NW elevation. The third sidestone on either side (to front of tomb) no longer bears the weight of the capstone. These two frontal sidestones are both quite low in height and have either sunken or may be broken, with that to SE protruding just above ground level. A large stone at the SW end of the NW side may also be displaced or may be part of an external layer of sidestones that no longer survive. An earthfast orthostat on the exterior of the SE side may also have formed part of an outer layer of orthostats. A large backstone is located in the centre at the NE end of the monument and the underside of rear capstone partially rests on it. There is some loose stone within the interior and it is otherwise obscured by vegetation. See De Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961 (attached) for plans and detailed measurements.
