At the top of a W-facing slope, in pasture overlooking Maryfort Lough to SW and Castle Lough to S, with good views across an undulating landscape, although inhibited by forestry in foreground to W and N. Depicted and named ‘Cromlech’ on all OS historic mapping. A rectangular area (3.7m E-W; 2.2m N-S) defined by two in situ, prostrate orthostats to S and two opposing sidestones which have fallen flat, outwards along the W end of the N side. An in situ sidestone forms the E-end of the N side. Three quite steadfast, rounded boulders are located at the E end of the S side. The interior is raised (H 0.2m) above the external ground level. A narrow view of the other smaller stones is seen under the raised side of the capstone. The capstone (L 2.3m ESE-WNW; Wth 2.05m NNE-SSW; T 0.24m) has fallen downwards to N and is tilted with its N side just above (H 0.3m) external ground level and the S side tilted upwards covering the interior of the monument and much higher (H 1m) above external ground level. The two largest orthostats bearing the weight of the capstone on the N side, have fallen outwards and are lying flat under the displaced capstone in both cases. Other small earthfast boulders and rocks are located immediately around the monument to S, W and N. A field boundary (long axis N-S) and a large oak tree directly abut the monument to E and it is likely that the lateral roots penetrate the monument. A thorn tree grows out of the exterior of the monument at S.

On a S-facing slope, in improved pasture, overlooking low-lying ground E-WNW, where there are moderate views. Not depicted on any OS historic mapping. A former standing stone which is now lying prostrate (L 2.3m) within a slight depression. Identified in 2004 when the stone is recorded as being upright (SMR file). In improved pasture, on a low rise of rock outcrop with reasonable views. The monument generally exists as described by De Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 76, No. 100). Depicted and named as ‘Giant’s Grave’ on 1921 edition OS 6-inch map. A rectangular area (2.2m NE-SW; 1.3m NW-SE) defined by an orthostat on three sides. The orthostat to SE (L 1.8m; T 0.3m; int. H 1.12m; ext. H 0.8m) and the orthostat to SW (L 1.9m; T 0.17m; int. H 1.05m; ext. H 0.8m) are of similar dimensions. A third, substantial orthostat (L 2.7m; T 0.27m; int. H 1.05m; ext. H 0.85m) defines the NW side of the monument. A bullaun stone (CL035-163----) partially closes the opening to NE, leaving a small gap (Wth 0.52m) at N. According to local information, this boulder previously lay adjacent to NE of the monument and was moved here to close the interior from animals. It may have come from a holy well (CL035-001----) 350m to the N. The NW and SE sidestones have tilted to SE under the weight of the substantial capstone (2.48m NE-SW; 2.45m NW-SE; T 0.4m) which is also tilting very slightly to SE. An outer orthostat (L 1.05m; T 0.2m; H 0.87m) is parallel to the main weight-bearing one and leans outwards at the NE end of the SE side; a smaller orthostat is adjacent, at the SW end and an even smaller example is located between the two. The space between the inner, weight-bearing orthosat and the three outer examples on the SE side, is filled with a compact earthen material and loose stones. The single orthostat forming the SW side does not appear to bear any weight of the capstone; a number of small stones are banked up against the exterior of this side. A pair of outer upright orthostats are located c. 0.72m from the main weight-bearing example forming the NW side. An orthostat (1.1m; T 0.37m; H 0.62m) extends (long-axis NE-SW) from the W-corner and according to De Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.) may be the sidestone of a portico. Two substantial slabs (L 2.0m; Wth 0.9m; T 0.31m) lie flat, adjacent to NW, with two smaller slabs further to NE, which appear to have previously formed part of the monument. The interior is generally level and contains occasional loose stones. According to De Valera and Ó Nualláin (ibid.), the associated mound (13.5m E-W; 7.5m N-S) is roughly circular in plan. A tree-lined field boundary is c. 1.8m to NNW and truncates the mound.

This feature, named as ‘Dermot and Grania’s Bed’ on the 1840 OS 6-inch map stood in gently undulating pasture, toward the top of a gentle SE-facing slope with limited views of the surrounding landscape. Westropp (1902-04, 112 (b)) drew a plan of the monument and described it as ‘a defaced little cist, 12 feet long and 4 feet 9 inches wide. The sides and ends remain; and a cover-slab, now partly buried, lies on the north-west slab. The south side lies ENE and WSW’. The monument is named as ‘Site of’ on the OS 25-inch map suggesting that it was no longer extant by the late 19th century. De Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 91, no. 2) describe it as the site of a probable wedge tomb. On inspection in 2017 there were no visible remains of any such features at ground level. The site of another wedge tomb (CL035-007----) is c. 55m to the S.

This feature, named ‘Dermot and Grania’s Bed’ on the 1840 edition of the OS 6-inch map, stood in a generally level area in an otherwise gently undulating field with reasonable views of the surrounding landscape. The field has some rock outcrop close to the surface. Described in the Ordnance Survey letters (OSL, vol. 2, 285) as being ‘in the form of an ordinary grave (coffin) measuring 19 feet 6 inches in length and 4 feet 5 inches in breadth at the foot, and 6 feet 4 inches in breadth at the head, the thickness of the stones all round being included in the measurement. This was enclosed by a number of large stones placed at a few feet distance, and following the form of the grave.’ It is described by Westropp (1902, 113, No. 25i) as a ‘cist….lying in the field near the junction of the by-road and the Tulla road….’. De Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 98), indicate that the tomb had been destroyed before Westropp’s visit, hence his reference to a ‘cist’. They noted several almost concealed blocks, obviously ‘not in-situ’ (ibid.). On inspection in 2017 there were no visible remains of any such features at ground level.

CL035-010----:
In improved pasture, at the ESE-end of a gently undulating ridge (long-axis c. E-W) with reasonable views of surrounding landscape. Listed as 'Enclosure' in the SMR (1992) and the RMP (1996). Depicted as a large circular enclosure (diam. c. 50m) on the 1840 edition of the OS 6-inch map and as a slightly smaller enclosure (c. 40m NW-SE; c. 35m NE-SW) on the OS 25-inch map. The enclosure is not depicted on the 1921 edition of the OS 6-inch map, suggesting that it had been levelled by the early 20th century. In 1997 a very broad low bank (Wth 9-13m) was noted by staff of the North Munster Project of the Discovery Programme giving an overall diam. of c. 52m. Inspection in 2017 revealed an oval area (32m N-S; 28m E-W) defined by a scarp (Wth 8m; H 0.25m) NE-E-SE with very little trace SE-S-WSW. There is an internal scarp (Wth 10m; H 0.4m) WSW-N, where it falls from an area of rock outcrop on the exterior, down into the W sector of the interior which is dish-shaped. The possible remains of an entrance (Wth c. 6m) are at W. Four megalithic tombs (CL035-009---, CL035-013002-, CL035-015----, CL035-011----) are situated within a 270m radius to E, ESE, SE and NW and several other similar megalithic monuments are located within the wider vicinity.
Compiled by: Mary Tunney and Alison McQueen
Date of upload: 7 November 2017
CL035-011----:
In improved pasture, on a very gentle ESE-facing slope with reasonable views. The monument survives as described by De Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, vol. 1, 78, no. 101). It is depicted and named as ‘Dermot & Grania’s Bed’ on all OS historic mapping and is shown on the 1840 edition of the OS 6-inch map within the rectangular plot of a small building. According to Curry in 1839 (OSL, vol. 2, 159), it once formed part of a pig-sty near Green’s House. A well-preserved wedge tomb (2.2m N-S; 3.15m E-W; max. H 1.3m) defined by an orthostat to N, S, E and W. The capstone is a substantial subrectangular megalith covered in sod (H 0.25m) which accentuates the height of the monument. The weight of the capstone is borne only by the N and S orthostats, which taper down slightly from W to E. A small pinning stone is lodged between the S orthostat and the underside of the capstone. The interior is a rectangular area (1.6m N-S; c. 2.26m E-W) which is open at the NE and SE corners where the orthostats do not touch. The base of the interior is flat and contains numerous loose stones, probably derived from modern field clearance. An embanked enclosure (CL035-010----) lies 80m to the NNW and the sites and scant remains of several megalithic tombs lie in the vicinity to N and E.

In improved pasture, on a generally level area of a gentle SW-facing slope with reasonable views of the surrounding landscape. This feature is not named on any OS historic mapping. Described as, ‘a possible standing stone (limestone) …located in the field wall (running SW-NE) at the inner edge of the bank of the levelled enclosure (CL035-013001-)’ (North Munster Project, Discovery Programme 1997). On inspection in 2017 there is no extant field wall at this location and there is no such standing stone visible at ground level. A levelled enclosure (CL035-013001-) is located c. 15m to NW and a megalithic structure (CL035-013003-) formerly stood c. 22m to W.

CL035-015----:
This feature, named as ‘Giant’s Grave’ on the 1840 edition OS 6-inch map, stood on a gentle SW-facing slope, in improved pasture with reasonable views of the surrounding landscape. The surface of this field is uneven and gently undulating suggesting that there is limestone rock outcrop close to the surface. Named ‘Giant’s Grave (site of)’ and no longer depicted on the 25-inch OS map. The monument not seen by Westropp (1902, 113), but he suggests a dark patch of grass in a small depression may mark the site. According to Curry in 1839 (OSL, vol. 2, 159 and 285) the monument was ‘in the form of an ordinary grave (coffin) measuring 19 feet six inches in length and 4 feet 5 inches in breadth at the foot and 6 feet four inches at the head, the thickness in the stones all round being included in the measurement. This was enclosed by a number of large stones placed at a few feet distance, and following the form of the grave’. On inspection in 2017 there were no visible remains of any such features at ground level. An enclosure (CL035-013001-), a megalithic structure (CL035-013002-) and a standing stone (CL035-013003-) are c. 55m to the NW. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1961, 92, no. 4)
Compiled by: Mary Tunney and Alison McQueen
Date of upload: 8 November 2017
CL035-034----:
On top of a small, low rise, in improved pasture and parkland of the former Maryfort Estate. Depicted on the 25-inch OS map as a small oval feature and depicted on the 1921 edition of the OS 6-inch map and named ‘Cromlech’. This monument appears to be the partially collapsed remains of a wedge tomb (overall dims. 1.9m NE-SW; 2.2m NW-SE; overall max. H 1.2m) now consisting of the NW sidestone (L 1.2m; Wth 1.1m; T 0.2m) and a substantial capstone (L 1.8m; Wth 1.7m; T 0.3m). The corner of a third, irregular-shaped stone (L 0.8m; Wth 0.4m; max. T 0.3m) is evident to the immediate S of the capstone. The monument would have been orientated long-axis NE-SW had the NE sidestone survived in situ. This has collapsed and the capstone has fallen on the NE side. There is a slight ‘mound’ under this end of the capstone and around it suggesting that the missing NE sidestone may be lying prostrate below the sod and vegetation. The visible orthostats are of a weathered limestone. The capstone is fractured and pitted with irregular solution marks upon its surface. The NW sidestone is smoother in comparison, although is cracked across the SW corner. De Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, No. 102) describe a circular mound (diam. c. 4.5m; H c. 1m) surrounding the tomb, however they acknowledge that most of this mound may not be original as it had been used to dump field clearance stones at the time of their survey. The monument is located within a modern square-plan enclosure (4.5m NE-SW; 4.5m NW-SE) defined by a timber fence, which is set c. 0.8-1.5m from the orthostats. A factory boundary is c. 22m to SE.

CL035-037----:
In an elevated area of deciduous woodland, overlooking lower ground to E and SE. This portal tomb appears to survive in a slightly more collapsed state than as described in previous accounts by Westropp (1902-04, 117-18) and De Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 78-9). Not depicted on OS historic mapping. A large, collapsed megalithic tomb (c. 5m NW-SE; c. 4m NE-SW; H c. 2m) (long-axis NW-SE) consisting of moss-covered limestones. The capstone (L 3.75m; Wth 2.8m; T 1.5m) is resting on one flat limestone (L 1.7m NW-SE; Wth 1.6m NE-SW; T 0.25m) at the SE end and is elevated 0.6m above ground level at the NW end. There is a flat stone at WNW (L 2.1m NW-SE; Wth 1.65m NE-SW; T 0.2m) and at N (L 2m NW-SE; Wth 1.3m NE-SW; T 0.2m) which are partially under the capstone. Two short upright stones and several other stones are also beneath, yet difficult to see. There is a possible collapsed opening at NW. An ivy-clad tree is abutting to SSW and it appears to be growing out of a natural erratic which has split into four parts. There are clusters of glacial erratics visible on this knoll to S, SE and E, with a very large cluster noted c. 40m to SE.

CL035-047----:
On a very gentle W-facing slope, in improved, gently undulating pasture with reasonable views of the surrounding low-lying landscape. The monument appears to exist as described by De Valera and Ó Nualláin (1961, 79, no. 104) and is depicted and named ‘Dermot & Grania’s Bed on OS historic mapping. The monument is marked by a distinct cluster of mature thorn trees and consists of the partially collapsed remains of a wedge tomb (4.8m NE-SW; 2.7m NW-SE) constructed of numerous orthostats some of which appear to be in situ and some which are slightly displaced due to potential collapse in antiquity, under the weight of the capstone. A perfectly upright, substantial orthostat (L 2.1m; T 0.4m; H 0.91m) forms the main portion of the SE side and a smaller, slightly NW-tilting orthostat (L 1.4m; min. T 0.3m; H 0.76m) forms the remainder of the SE side, having collapsed slightly inwards. The NW side is formed by two parallel, collapsed orthostats (inner stone L 0.68m; T 0.15m; H 0.17m; outer stone L 0.87m; T 0.16m; H 0.3m), which have fallen outwards. The remainder of the NW side is formed by a long orthostat (L 1.5m; T 0.2m; Wth 1.2m) which has collapsed inwards. A small orthostat (L 0.53m; T 0.17m; H 0.28m) is to the rear on this side, which has also fallen outwards slightly. A substantial capstone forms the roof over the main portion of the tomb, at the NE end. It does not have any weight bearing upon the largest of the orthostats on the SE-side, which may account for collapse of the two parallel orthostats on the opposite side to NW. The orthostats defining the NW (1.35m; T 0.35m; H 0.44m) and SE sides of the tomb at the SW end, have both collapsed inwards under the weight of a second capstone (L 1.5m; Wth 1.12m; T 0.35m). This second, smaller capstone partially rests upon the larger capstone, where they overlap. A third capstone-like megalith (L 1.5m; Wth 1.1m; T 0.3m) lies against the SW end of the tomb and appears to be ex situ, having once formed part of the monument. A second, potentially ex situ stone (L 1.05m; Wth 0.96m; T 0.23m) is adjacent to the tomb at NW. The monument was not seen at the NE end, due to a dense growth of briars.

CL035-146----:
On top of a knoll, in rough pasture, with land sloping down steeply to NW and NE. There are reasonable views of the surrounding landscape including mountains in the distance to E. This wedge tomb is not depicted on any of the OS historic mapping. It was identified during a survey carried out for the East Clare Community Co-Op, Scarriff (Paul Walsh OSi pers. comm., 1995). The monument consists of a raised, rectangular area (2.5m E-W; 2m N-S) enclosed by three prostrate stones set upright and defining the S side (L 1.55m; T 0.35m; H 0.6m), W side (L 1.5m; T 0.3m; H 0.8m) and N side (L 1.3m; T 0.25m; H 0.65m). The monument is open to E. The stones to S and N are slanting to S and that to W is slanting to W. Other components of the monument may be sod covered within the raised interior (H 0.5m). A large boulder (L 1.3m; T 0.9m; H 0.45m) is located c. 6m to NE and may have formed part of the monument. A substantial stone (L 1.9m; Wth 1.35m; T 0.6m) which is located on top of the field boundary, c. 34m to WSW, may also have formed part of the monument, potentially as a capstone, being of the same type of weathered limestone.

In a flat field of rushes overlooked by a ridge to N. A flat, thin standing stone (max. H 2.05m; Wth c. 0.4m; T c. 0.15m ) oriented NE-SW. The top slopes and is slightly higher at the NE end. The stone leans slightly to the SE. In 2003 a small set stone was noted at the base. A ringfort (CL056-044----) is c. 110m to the SW.
